sweeps.topic: vsp-recon — Virtual surgical planning & reconstruction for head & neck (open-source mandible/fibula/maxilla/orbit planning, automated osteotomy planning, STL & point-of-care 3D printing)

findings.title: SlicerBoneReconstructionPlanner (BRP) — 3D Slicer module for fibula-flap mandible reconstruction planning + cutting-guide generation
findings.summary: Maintained SlicerIGT extension: segment mandible + fibula, lay a mandibular reconstruction curve, auto-seed osteotomy planes from that curve, simulate the neomandible, and generate miter-box fibula guides and saw-box mandible guides, all exportable as STL. BSD-3-Clause. Fibula centerline is auto-generated and user-editable. Note: SlicerVESPA binaries it can use derive from GPLv3 CGAL code (not redistributed by BRP itself).
findings.relevance: Direct reference implementation for roadmap item 9 (mandible planner: canal, osteotomies, fibula segments) and item 6 (segmentation → STL). The plane-from-curve seeding logic, miter-box guide geometry, and the neomandible assembly are the exact algorithms HNRad would otherwise invent. BSD-3 means the approach (and, with attribution, code) can be ported to a Python/VTK backend. Also a realistic 'escape hatch': recommend Slicer+BRP for actual guide fabrication while HNRad does the diagnostic/measurement half.
findings.feasibility: Slicer itself is a portable ZIP install (no admin) on Windows; BRP needs Slicer 5.x, not a pip package. For HNRad, the reusable part is the geometry math (VTK plane clipping, centerline resampling, boolean-free miter boxes) which reimplements cleanly on CPU with vtk/SimpleITK. Python 3.13 note: Slicer ships its own Python, so no conflict.

findings.title: BoneReconstructionPlanner: open-source virtual surgical planning and surgical guide generation for mandibular reconstruction (Maisi et al.)
findings.summary: The methods/validation paper behind the BRP Slicer extension, published in Annals of 3D Printed Medicine. Describes the planning workflow, guide design and reported sub-millimetre planning accuracy. Citation was retrieved from the extension's own README rather than from the publisher page directly.
findings.relevance: Citable provenance for anything HNRad borrows from BRP, and a template for how to report accuracy of an in-house planner (planned-vs-achieved segment length, intergonial/intercondylar distances).
findings.feasibility: n/a — I resolved this DOI from the BRP repository README, not from the publisher page, so treat the exact volume/pages as unverified.

findings.title: Automated planning of mandible reconstruction with fibula free flap based on shape completion and morphometric descriptors
findings.summary: Two-step fully automated FFF planning framework: a 3D generative shape-completion model reconstructs the premorbid mandible from the partial/defect mandible, then novel 2D morphometric descriptors define an objective function over the osteotomy/splice/placement parameters that is optimized to find the best shape-matched plan. Retrospective 65-patient tumour cohort; qualitative and quantitative results favourable vs experienced clinicians' plans, and user-independent. DOI 10.1016/j.media.2025.103544.
findings.relevance: This is the state of the art for roadmap item 9's hardest sub-problem: where to put the osteotomies. Even without their generative model, the morphometric-descriptor objective function (a small set of interpretable 2D variables + a scalar cost) is implementable in NumPy/SciPy on CPU and would let HNRad rank candidate segment plans rather than just display them.
findings.feasibility: No public repo located. The shape-completion generator would need a GPU to train but CPU inference of a small 3D generative model on a decimated mandible mesh is plausible; the optimization half (descriptors + objective) is pure geometry and fully CPU-feasible in Python 3.13.

findings.title: A Mandibular Defect Dataset for Autonomous Reconstruction Planning in Oral and Maxillofacial Surgery
findings.summary: First clinically derived mandibular defect dataset: 147 defect models manually annotated by experienced surgeons to clinical standards, capturing realistic defect boundaries and per-patient anatomy. Critically, each defect model ships with its HCL (Jewer–Boyd hemimandibular/central/lateral) classification diagnosis plus associated metadata. Scientific Data, DOI 10.1038/s41597-025-06048-8.
findings.relevance: The only public resource found that pairs defect geometry with HCL labels — directly usable to build and validate an automatic HCL classifier and defect-length calculator for HNRad's mandible planner. Also a ready-made test set for any resection/osteotomy planning code without touching PHI.
findings.license: Scientific Data data descriptors are normally CC BY 4.0, but confirm the repository record's own terms before redistribution
findings.feasibility: Meshes/labels only — no inference required. Loads with trimesh or vtk on CPU; ideal as an offline fixture set for HNRad unit tests on a locked-down workstation (download once, then fully local).

findings.title: OsteoOpt / OsteoOpt++ — patient-specific mandibular reconstruction optimization with predicted bone union
findings.summary: UBC (Prisman/Fels/Hodgson) image-to-decision planner: builds a personalized model from preop CT, runs ArtiSynth biomechanical chewing simulation, and uses Bayesian optimization (expected-improvement-plus) over six surgical variables to maximize bone apposition at graft interfaces subject to safety. Reports up to 29 pp improvement in donor–mandible apposition vs surgeon plans and 70–85% overlap with actual year-1 bone formation. Preprint arXiv:2605.01084; Medical Image Analysis 2026.
findings.relevance: Shows the next step past geometric planning — scoring a plan by predicted union, not just symmetry. The apposition-area metric (contact surface between adjacent fibula segments and between fibula and native mandible) is a cheap, high-value number HNRad could compute per candidate plan with pure mesh geometry, no simulation.
findings.license: PolyForm Noncommercial License 1.0.0 — research/education only; commercial use requires written permission. Flag clearly: NOT permissive.
findings.feasibility: Heavy stack: Java/JDK 8+ + ArtiSynth + MATLAB optimization scripts + Python 3.8 + Slicer/TotalSegmentator. Tested on Windows but MATLAB and the Java sim make it impractical to vendor into HNRad. Borrow the metric definitions, not the code. Python 3.8 requirement conflicts with 3.13.

findings.title: SlicerOrbitSurgerySim — open-source virtual registration and quantitative comparison of preformed orbital plates
findings.summary: 3D Slicer extension (Zhang, Gunn, Read-Fuller) letting a surgeon interactively register and compare multiple preformed orbital plates against a patient-specific orbit, producing reproducible plate-to-orbit distance metrics and supporting population-level analysis of implant adaptability. Code, sample datasets and tutorials at github.com/chz31/SlicerOrbitSurgerySim. Published in J Oral Maxillofac Surg 2026.
findings.relevance: The closest open-source analogue for the orbital/midface side of HNRad's reconstruction ambitions (Brown class III maxillectomy with orbital floor). The plate-to-surface distance map is the same computation HNRad would need for any 'does this implant fit' or 'how far is the reconstruction from the mirrored contralateral orbit' feature.
findings.license: Not stated in the abstract/preprint I retrieved — check the repository LICENSE before reuse
findings.feasibility: Slicer extension, so Python + VTK under the hood; the distance-metric core is CPU-only and portable. Mirroring + closest-point distance on meshes is trivially feasible with vtk/scipy.spatial on the target workstation.

findings.title: DentalSegmentator — open-source nnU-Net model for CT/CBCT segmentation of maxilla, mandible, upper/lower teeth and mandibular canal
findings.summary: Trained on 470 dental CT/CBCT scans, evaluated on 256 scans from seven institutions. Segments five structures: maxilla/upper skull, mandible, upper teeth, lower teeth, and the inferior alveolar (mandibular) canal. Distributed as a 3D Slicer extension with weights auto-downloaded, also on GitHub Releases and Zenodo (record 10829675) for direct command-line nnU-Net use. Published in Journal of Dentistry 2024.
findings.relevance: Highest-value single adoption for HNRad roadmap items 9 and 13: it gives the mandible surface AND the mandibular canal automatically — the canal is the safety structure the mandible planner must show, and hand-segmenting it is the main reason surgeons skip in-house planning. Feeds directly into osteotomy planning and STL export.
findings.license: Code repo has a LICENSE file (verify text); Zenodo weights appear to be Creative Commons Attribution (CC BY) — permissive for local clinical/research use with attribution, but confirm before any redistribution
findings.feasibility: Strong fit: the README explicitly states it runs on CPU (slower without CUDA) and recommends 32 GB RAM — exactly Brian's box (UHD 770, 32 GB). Runs via nnU-Net v2 from PyPI, so install into a separate Python 3.11 venv (nnU-Net/torch wheels for 3.13 are the risk) with CPU-only torch. Weights download once, then fully offline — nothing leaves the device.
findings.venue_or_repo: GitHub gaudot/SlicerDentalSegmentator; Zenodo 10829675; Journal of Dentistry

findings.title: Automated segmentation of the fibula from CT using two-stepped 3D U-Nets
findings.summary: Fully automatic CNN pipeline for fibula segmentation from CT, using a two-step 3D U-Net (coarse localization then fine segmentation). Best model reached mean Dice 0.95 with average surface distance below 0.31 mm in the surgically relevant region of interest. Scientific Reports 2025.
findings.relevance: The donor-side half of roadmap item 9. If HNRad ever ingests a CT angiogram of the lower extremity, this removes the fibula segmentation step; the two-stage coarse-to-fine design is also the right pattern for CPU inference (small ROI in step two keeps memory and time bounded).
findings.license: Scientific Reports is CC BY; weight/code availability not confirmed in what I retrieved
findings.feasibility: Two-stage design is the key CPU-feasibility trick — the fine model only sees a cropped ROI. Whether pretrained weights are released was not confirmed; if only the architecture is published this is reference-only for HNRad (no local training capacity on UHD 770).

findings.title: Accuracy and Clinical Outcomes of Mandibular Reconstruction Using Fibula Free Flaps and Open-Source Virtual Surgical Planning
findings.summary: 25 consecutive FFF patients (2021–2025) planned entirely in 3D Slicer + Blender with 3D-printed reference models and freehand osteotomies (no cutting guides). Planned-vs-postop CT linear deviations 1.53–3.05 mm; small but significant differences in intercondylar distance, intergonial distance and fibula segment length; no significant difference in AP distance or gonial angle. 100% flap survival, one minor complication. DOI 10.1097/SCS.0000000000013058.
findings.relevance: The clinical evidence that a free/open planning stack — exactly HNRad's ambition — produces clinically acceptable accuracy. Also hands HNRad its validation metric set: intercondylar, intergonial, AP distance, gonial angle, per-segment fibula length. Those five measurements should be first-class outputs of the mandible planner.
findings.feasibility: n/a — clinical series. The five cephalometric metrics are all computable from landmarks on a mandible mesh with NumPy on CPU.

findings.title: In-house VSP and guided mandibular reconstruction is less precise, but more economical and time-efficient than commercial procedures (Block et al.)
findings.summary: Head & Neck 2024 head-to-head of in-house versus commercial VSP for guided mandibular reconstruction on postoperative reconstruction accuracy and economics. Conclusion in the title: in-house is measurably less precise but cheaper and faster (no vendor turnaround).
findings.relevance: The honest counterweight for HNRad's scope decisions. It argues HNRad should be explicit that it is a planning/measurement aid, and that if guide fabrication precision is the goal, the accuracy gap versus a commercial VSP vendor must be disclosed. Useful framing for any tumor-board or IRB conversation.
findings.feasibility: n/a

findings.title: Training OMFS residents in VSP: open-source freeware vs commercial software for mandibular reconstruction with FFF
findings.summary: Ghent feasibility study. Five VSP-naive CMF residents each planned four FFF cases in both 3D Slicer + Blender (OSF) and Materialise Mimics/ProPlan CMF/3-Matic (CAS). CAS: 91 ± 15 min, 2325 ± 86 mouse clicks; OSF: 111 ± 26 min, 1876 ± 632 clicks. System Usability Scale 67.5 for CAS vs 50 for OSF. Concludes OSF is a cost-effective training alternative. DOI 10.3390/cmtr18010010.
findings.relevance: Quantifies exactly the usability gap HNRad exists to close: open-source is only ~20 min slower but scores 17.5 SUS points worse. An SUS of 50 is 'poor'. This is the strongest argument for HNRad's purpose-built UI over telling surgeons to learn raw Slicer+Blender, and it gives a concrete benchmark (beat SUS 67.5, stay under 90 min) to design against.
findings.feasibility: n/a — human-factors study. The click-count and time-per-step methodology is directly reusable to benchmark HNRad against Slicer.

findings.title: In-House Virtual Surgery Planning and 3D Printing for Head and Neck Surgery With Free Software: Our Workflow
findings.summary: Spanish university-hospital description of a complete in-house CAD/CAM pipeline for head and neck oncologic surgery using only free software — 3D Slicer for segmentation and model generation, Blender for guide design — plus in-house 3D printing of biomodels and mandible/fibula cutting guides. Emphasis on a cost-effective, time-efficient step-by-step workflow.
findings.relevance: Effectively a written spec for the pipeline HNRad is automating: which segmentation thresholds, which mesh operations, which export formats, what the printing step needs. Open access, so the full step list is readable and can be encoded as HNRad's default parameters.
findings.license: PMC open access (check article's CC terms)
findings.feasibility: n/a — workflow paper. Every step described is CPU-only and reproducible with SimpleITK + vtk + trimesh on the target workstation.

findings.title: Maxillomandibular Reconstruction Using Insourced Virtual Surgical Planning and Homemade CAD/CAM: A Single-Center Evolution in 75 Patients
findings.summary: KU Leuven series of 75 consecutive maxillofacial reconstructions (2015–2020) with a fully insourced VSP and 'home-made' CAD/CAM protocol across fibula, iliac crest and scapular angle flaps, evolving toward occlusion-based planning with immediate osseointegrated implants. Bone flap survival 94.7% at 4 months; 3-year patient survival 77.6%. Includes the financial balance of the in-house programme. DOI 10.1097/PRS.0000000000010142.
findings.relevance: Largest in-house VSP outcome series found, and the only one that covers iliac crest and scapular angle as well as fibula — relevant if HNRad's donor-site model should not be fibula-only. Also the reference for occlusion-driven planning (jaw-in-a-day), which changes where the osteotomies go.
findings.feasibility: n/a

findings.title: Medical 3D printing with a focus on point-of-care in cranio- and maxillofacial surgery: a systematic review
findings.summary: Systematic review across four databases, January 2018 – December 2020, 75 included studies, comparing external-laboratory versus point-of-care fabrication for CMF 3D printing applications. Provides the published-evidence landscape for in-hospital printing of biomodels, guides and implants.
findings.relevance: The evidence base to cite when justifying a point-of-care planning tool at all. Defines the application categories (anatomic model, cutting guide, patient-specific implant, occlusal splint) that HNRad's STL export should target.
findings.feasibility: n/a

findings.title: Controversies in point-of-care 3D printing for oncological and reconstructive surgery with free software in OMFS: European regulations, costs, and timeframe
findings.summary: Analyses the regulatory, cost and turnaround realities of point-of-care 3D printing with free software. Reported timeframe 2 weeks via biomedical industry versus 72 hours point-of-care; cost analysis found the cheapest free-software setup amortizes before the ninth case. Also addresses the EU MDR in-house exemption question for patient-specific devices.
findings.relevance: The regulatory reality check for HNRad. If HNRad ever emits an STL that gets printed and taken to the OR, it is arguably an in-house manufactured medical device. This paper frames that boundary. Practical mitigation for HNRad: keep planning/measurement outputs clearly separate from guide geometry, and label exports as non-clinical unless the institution has an in-house device programme.
findings.license: n/a (Elsevier; Int J Oral Maxillofac Surg)
findings.feasibility: n/a — regulatory/economic analysis, EU-centric; US FDA in-house 3D printing guidance would need separate review.
findings.venue_or_repo: International Journal of Oral and Maxillofacial Surgery

findings.title: Maxillectomy Guided by 3D Printing Versus Conventional Surgery for Patients with Head and Neck Cancer
findings.summary: Comparative study of 3D-printing-guided versus conventional maxillectomy. The guided group had a higher negative-margin rate (81.3% vs 76.9%) and trends toward better 5-year local recurrence-free survival (87.5% vs 58.7%) and overall survival (84.4% vs 70.1%); none of the differences reached statistical significance.
findings.relevance: One of the few papers linking VSP to an oncologic endpoint rather than a geometric one, for the maxillectomy side. Relevant to any HNRad claim about resection-plane planning, and a caution that the survival signal is a trend, not proof.
findings.feasibility: n/a

findings.title: Reconstruction techniques of the orbit after Brown class III maxillectomy: a systematic review (Dugast et al.)
findings.summary: Systematic review of orbital reconstruction options following Brown class III maxillectomy — the defect class where the orbital floor and the lower orbit are resected and reconstruction choice drives globe position and diplopia.
findings.relevance: Defines the Brown classification vocabulary HNRad should use for maxillary defects (vertical class I–VI, horizontal a–d), the midface analogue of HCL for the mandible. If HNRad adds a maxillary defect mapper, Brown class is the output label surgeons expect.
findings.feasibility: n/a

findings.title: Aesthetic and accuracy outcomes of maxillary defect reconstruction by 3D virtual surgical planning
findings.summary: VSP versus freehand for maxillary reconstruction. In vertical Brown class III cases, mean orbit height difference was 1.78 ± 1.33 mm with VSP versus 4.25 ± 0.95 mm freehand, and mean orbit volume difference 2.04 ± 0.85 cm³ versus 3.25 ± 0.17 cm³.
findings.relevance: Gives concrete, computable accuracy endpoints for midface/orbit planning — orbital height and orbital volume — both of which HNRad could compute from a segmented orbit versus the mirrored contralateral side with simple CPU geometry. That mirror-and-compare feature is a low-effort, high-clinical-value addition to roadmap item 6.
findings.feasibility: n/a for the study; the derived metrics (orbital volume from a closed surface, orbital height from landmarks) are straightforward with vtkMassProperties / trimesh on CPU.

findings.title: Intraoperative Real-Time Image-Guided Fibular Harvest and Mandibular Reconstruction: A Feasibility Study on Cadaveric Specimens (Prisman group, UBC)
findings.summary: Five cadaveric mandibulectomy + fibular reconstructions performed with a purpose-built image-guided surgery system (custom mandible/fibula fixation devices with navigation reference frames plus bespoke IGS software), replacing cutting guides. Planned-vs-actual mandible reconstruction Dice 0.80 ± 0.08 and Hausdorff-95 7.29 ± 4.81 mm; intercoronoid width 1.15 ± 1.17 mm, interangle width 0.90 ± 0.56 mm, projection 1.47 ± 1.62 mm. DOI 10.1002/hed.27954.
findings.relevance: Establishes the accuracy vocabulary HNRad should adopt for reporting plan-vs-outcome: Dice plus HD95 on the reconstructed mandible, alongside the three cephalometric widths. Also a realistic ceiling — even a dedicated navigation rig lands at HD95 ~7 mm, which is useful for setting honest expectations on any HNRad measurement.
findings.feasibility: n/a — cadaveric. Dice/HD95 between two meshes or label maps is cheap on CPU via SimpleITK or scikit-image.

findings.title: vtk-js + itk-wasm — browser-native mesh/STL pipeline for a Cornerstone3D app
findings.summary: VTK.js is the ES6 port of VTK for the browser; its pipeline covers ImageData and PolyData plus readers/writers for STL, OBJ, VTP and VTI, and recent releases added itk-wasm interop for loading meshes and geometry. Cornerstone3D's rendering engine is already built on vtk-js. Kitware also ships itk-vtk-viewer (BSD 3-clause) as a reference integration.
findings.relevance: Means HNRad does not need a Python round-trip for the reconstruction geometry: marching-cubes surfaces, plane clipping for osteotomies, mesh transforms for placing fibula segments, and STL export can all run client-side in the existing React + Cornerstone3D viewer, keeping data in-browser and satisfying the local-only constraint with zero server compute. Serves roadmap items 3, 6 and 9.
findings.feasibility: Excellent for this workstation: WebGL/WASM in the browser sidesteps the lack of CUDA entirely, and npm install under Node 20 is user-level. No admin rights, no Python version constraint. Main cost is JS memory limits on very large volumes — decimate meshes before export.

findings.title: cs3d-viewer — Cornerstone3D MPR + VTK.js meshing + WASM DICOM-SEG-to-STL reference app
findings.summary: Web-native 2D/3D DICOM workstation combining Cornerstone3D MPR, VTK.js 3D meshing and dual AI backends (TotalSegmentator and MONAI) for organ volumetry and lesion detection. Notably uses PolySeg WASM acceleration for client-side conversion of DICOM SEG label maps into 3D surface meshes, with one-click export of segmented structures to printable .stl.
findings.relevance: A working reference for exactly HNRad's stack — the label-map-to-mesh-to-STL path entirely client side, which is the bridge between roadmap item 6 (segmentation/volumetrics/STL) and item 9 (mandible planner). Worth reading for the PolySeg WASM wiring and the AI-backend integration pattern even if the app itself is not adopted.
findings.license: Not verified — check the repository LICENSE; this is an individual's project, not an institutionally maintained one
findings.feasibility: Same stack as HNRad (React/Cornerstone3D/VTK.js/Node 20), so it installs at user level with no admin. Its AI backends assume a TotalSegmentator/MONAI service, which on CPU-only hardware will be slow; treat the viewer/meshing half as the reusable part.

findings.title: SlicerCMF — craniomaxillofacial module suite for 3D Slicer (DCBIA-OrthoLab)
findings.summary: Curated 3D Slicer extension bundling CMF-specific image analysis modules for patient-specific decision making and longitudinal assessment via registration of serial scans, with a published description of the module suite (PMC7786614). Project site cmf.slicer.org.
findings.relevance: Relevant to roadmap item 11 (compare mode with registration) applied to the facial skeleton — serial-scan registration and shape-change quantification are already solved here. Also a map of which CMF analyses the academic community considers worth having, which is a useful checklist against HNRad's feature list.
findings.license: 3D Slicer ecosystem is typically BSD-style; verify the repository LICENSE per module (some DCBIA modules wrap third-party code)
findings.feasibility: Slicer extension, portable install without admin. Modules are Python/VTK so individual algorithms are portable, but the suite is dental/orthodontic-leaning rather than oncologic H&N.

findings.title: An Automated Framework for Mandibular Reconstruction: Evaluation and Clinical Application (Li et al.)
findings.summary: Head & Neck 2026 paper presenting an automated mandibular reconstruction framework with evaluation and clinical application. I located this record in search results but the publisher page returned HTTP 403, so I could not verify the methods, accuracy figures, or whether code is released.
findings.relevance: Would be the most recent clinical validation of end-to-end automated mandible reconstruction planning (roadmap item 9) if the numbers hold up. Flagged for follow-up via institutional access rather than accepted as evidence.
findings.feasibility: n/a — could not retrieve. Treat title and venue as the only verified facts.

findings.title: Deep ensemble learning-driven fully automated multi-structure segmentation for precision craniomaxillofacial surgery
findings.summary: Deep ensemble approach to fully automated multi-structure CMF segmentation intended to support precision craniomaxillofacial surgical planning. Open access via PMC. I confirmed the record exists in search results but did not retrieve the full methods, so the exact structure list and Dice figures are unverified.
findings.relevance: Candidate second option alongside DentalSegmentator for automatic bony CMF segmentation feeding HNRad's mandible/maxilla planning. Ensembles are a poor fit for CPU-only inference though (N-fold the runtime), so this is likely reference rather than adopt on this hardware.
findings.feasibility: Ensemble inference multiplies CPU cost; on UHD 770 with no CUDA a single nnU-Net pass is already minutes-scale, so an ensemble is probably impractical for interactive use. Prefer single-model DentalSegmentator.

gaps: Could not verify the Maisi et al. BoneReconstructionPlanner validation paper directly at the publisher — the DOI (10.1016/j.stlm.2023.100109) came from the extension's own README, so volume/pages and the reported accuracy figures are unconfirmed.

Could not retrieve Li et al. 2026 'An Automated Framework for Mandibular Reconstruction' (Head & Neck, hed.70215) — publisher returned HTTP 403. Its accuracy numbers and any code release remain unknown.

No open-source tool was found that automatically computes defect length or assigns an HCL (Jewer-Boyd) class from a segmented mandible. The Sci Data defect dataset supplies HCL labels, but the classifier itself does not appear to exist publicly — this looks like a genuine gap HNRad could fill cheaply.

Licenses are unverified for SlicerOrbitSurgerySim, cs3d-viewer, and the exact LICENSE.txt text in SlicerDentalSegmentator's repo (only the Zenodo weights appeared to be CC BY). These need checking before any code reuse.

Could not confirm whether pretrained weights are publicly released for the two-step fibula segmentation 3D U-Net (Sci Rep 2025) — if only the architecture is published, it is unusable on this hardware since local training is not possible.

No measured CPU inference times found for DentalSegmentator on Intel integrated graphics — the README says CPU works but is 'significantly slower' without a number. Needs an empirical timing test on the actual workstation before committing to it in an interactive workflow.

Did not investigate US FDA guidance on in-house / point-of-care 3D printed patient-matched devices; the regulatory paper found is EU MDR-focused. This matters if HNRad ever exports guide geometry rather than diagnostic measurements.

No open-source implementation of the Guo et al. shape-completion premorbid mandible model was found, and no public search was done for scapula or iliac-crest donor-site planning code (the Vranckx series covers them clinically but not computationally).
Did not search for VSP work specific to jaw-in-a-day / immediate dental implant placement geometry beyond two case-level papers, so the occlusion-driven planning literature is underexplored.

findings.title: OHIF Viewer v3 (Open Health Imaging Foundation)
findings.summary: Zero-footprint web DICOM viewer built on Cornerstone3D. Ships extensions for DICOM SEG rendering + export, RTSTRUCT rendering, DICOM SR, measurement tracking across timepoints, and a Total Metabolic Tumor Volume (TMTV) mode; MPR, MIP, labelmap and contour segmentation rendering, whole-slide and PDF/video. Requires Node 18+, Yarn workspaces. Architecture = extensions + modes + services (ExtensionManager registry).
findings.relevance: Direct architectural template for nearly every HNRad roadmap item. Borrow its mode/extension split (a 'H&N mode' per workflow), its measurement-tracking extension for (4), its SEG extension for (6), its TMTV mode for (12), and its compare/registration hanging protocols for (11). MIT license allows lifting code outright.
findings.feasibility: Node 20 is fine. Runs fully offline against local static DICOMweb or a local file datasource — no data leaves the box. Rendering is WebGL2 on the Intel UHD 770; heavy MPR/VR will be the bottleneck, not the framework.

findings.title: OHIF Hanging Protocol module / HangingProtocolService
findings.summary: Declarative JSON protocol engine: matching rules on study/series/instance metadata select a layout, assign displaySets to viewports, and fire callbacks at protocol stages. Supports multi-stage protocols (e.g. axial-only → 3-up MPR → fusion) and runtime stage switching.
findings.relevance: Exactly the mechanism HNRad needs for automatic H&N layouts: neck CT-with-contrast → axial/coronal/sagittal MPR; PET/CT → fusion 2x2 (item 12); prior + current → compare mode (item 11). Copy the protocol schema rather than inventing layout logic.
findings.feasibility: Pure config/JS, no GPU or Python cost. Usable even if you do not adopt the rest of OHIF — the matching-rule pattern ports cleanly to a bespoke Cornerstone3D app.

findings.title: Cornerstone3D (core, tools, adapters, dicomImageLoader)
findings.summary: TypeScript medical-imaging framework: WebGL2 GPU rendering, WASM image decoding, StackViewport + VolumeViewport (MPR) + 3D volume-rendering viewport, annotation/measurement tools, labelmap + contour + surface segmentation representations, and adapters for DICOM SEG and RTSTRUCT. Renders offscreen into one shared WebGL canvas and blits to on-screen canvases so viewports share GPU textures.
findings.relevance: Already the chosen viewer layer. The shared-texture design is what makes 3-up MPR plus a 3D view affordable on integrated graphics. Segmentation representations + SEG/RTSTRUCT adapters cover item (6) round-trip; annotation tools are the base for items (4), (5) carotid angle measurement and (8) CSA overlays.
findings.feasibility: Runs on Intel UHD 770 via WebGL2 — no CUDA needed. pnpm/Node 20, user-level. Verify UHD 770 WebGL limits before committing to large volumes.

findings.title: Cornerstone3D hard limit: MAX_3D_TEXTURE_SIZE = 2048 (issue #1360)
findings.summary: Reported failure 'Desired resource size is greater than max texture size' / 'texImage3D: width, height or depth out of range' when a volume or segmentation labelmap exceeds the 2048 3D-texture dimension cap. Cornerstone3D streams images to the GPU on demand and stores voxels in native dtype via a VoxelManager rather than caching float32, but the per-axis texture cap still applies.
findings.relevance: Critical feasibility constraint for HNRad. Thin-slice neck CT (0.5 mm, 600-1200 slices) plus a labelmap of the same geometry can approach the cap in the slice axis, and the Intel UHD 770 driver's reported MAX_3D_TEXTURE_SIZE may be lower than 2048. Plan for axial sub-volume cropping to the neck and downsampling for the 3D/VR view (item 3) and for AI segmentation output (items 6, 13).
findings.feasibility: Test early: read gl.MAX_3D_TEXTURE_SIZE and gl.MAX_TEXTURE_SIZE on the actual workstation before designing the volume pipeline.

findings.title: OHIF issue #3082 — support for extremely large volumes and 4D
findings.summary: Tracking issue documenting how OHIF/Cornerstone3D handle volumes too large for GPU memory, and the strategies considered (progressive/streaming load, native-dtype textures, decimation). Useful as a written record of the failure modes and the mitigations the maintainers actually shipped.
findings.relevance: Read before building the MPR (item 2) and volume rendering (item 3) layers so HNRad's loader adopts progressive loading and dtype-preserving textures from day one rather than retrofitting them after the first 1000-slice neck CTA fails to load.
findings.feasibility: Design reference only; no runtime cost.

findings.title: OHIF v3.10 — in-browser AI segmentation (SAM Labelmap Assist, WebGPU GrowCut)
findings.summary: Adds fully client-side AI segmentation: a Segment Anything (SAM) 'Labelmap Assist' that propagates a segmentation to the next/previous slice, include/exclude prompt-point segmentation, a WebGPU 3D GrowCut tool, brush preview with accept/edit/reject, morphological slice interpolation, automatic per-segment statistics (volume, voxel intensity, centroid, SUVpeak) and bidirectional measurement from the largest segment area, plus viewport undo/redo.
findings.relevance: The single highest-leverage find for HNRad items (6) segmentation+volumetrics and (13) AI segmentation: it proves interactive AI segmentation can run entirely in-browser with no server and no data egress. Per-segment volume + SUVpeak stats also directly serve item (12) MTV/SUV.
findings.feasibility: SAM-class models in-browser on a UHD 770 will be slow but workable for 2D slice prompts; the WebGPU GrowCut path needs Chrome/Edge WebGPU enabled, which may or may not be permitted by KP policy — verify chrome://gpu on the actual box.

findings.title: LesionTracker: Extensible Open-Source Zero-Footprint Web Viewer for Cancer Imaging Research and Clinical Trials
findings.summary: According to PubMed (PMID 29092955), Urban, Ziegler, Hafey, Harris et al. describe the OHIF-derived oncology viewer: protocol-driven lesion measurement, longitudinal timepoint comparison, and enforcement of response-criteria workflows in a zero-footprint browser viewer designed to be embedded in third-party informatics platforms.
findings.relevance: The published rationale and data model behind OHIF's measurement-tracking extension. Its timepoint/lesion schema is a ready-made model for HNRad's compare mode (item 11) and for structured tumor-board export (item 14).
findings.feasibility: n/a — design/provenance reference.

findings.title: 3D Slicer
findings.summary: Free open-source desktop platform for visualization, segmentation, registration and analysis of 3D medical images and meshes, with a full Python API, an extension manager, and a large ecosystem of clinical extensions. Effectively a free radiology workstation that is not tied to hardware, and a prototyping platform for new quantitative methods.
findings.relevance: Use as the ground-truth bench and algorithm source, not as the product. Prototype items (5)-(10) in Slicer Python first (fast iteration, mature widgets), then port the validated numerics into the FastAPI/SimpleITK backend. Slicer's Segment Editor effects, Segment Statistics module (volumetrics) and model/STL export are direct analogues of item (6).
findings.feasibility: Windows install without admin is the open question — prefer the archive/portable extraction or a per-user install directory. CPU-only rendering works. Python API is Slicer's own bundled interpreter, not your 3.13 venv.

findings.title: 3D Slicer as an image computing platform for the Quantitative Imaging Network
findings.summary: According to PubMed (PMID 22770690), Fedorov, Beichel, Kalpathy-Cramer, Pieper, Kikinis et al. present 3D Slicer as a platform for prototyping, developing and evaluating quantitative image-analysis tools, with QIN use cases and an argument for the extension model. Seminal, heavily cited; MeSH terms include Head and Neck Neoplasms.
findings.relevance: The canonical citation for 'why an extensible imaging platform' — useful framing for HNRad's own architecture and for any internal write-up or IRB/validation document justifying a locally built quantitative tool.
findings.feasibility: n/a

findings.title: SlicerExtension-VMTK — Extract Centerline & Cross-Section Analysis
findings.summary: Brings the Vascular Modeling Toolkit into Slicer. The rewritten Extract Centerline module does fast, robust centerline extraction for vessel/airway/any tubular tree, and the Cross-Section Analysis module computes and plots/tabulates local cross-sectional area along the centerline — either via maximum-inscribed-sphere radius (MISR) or by slicing the surface perpendicular to the centerline and triangulating.
findings.relevance: Highest-value single component for roadmap item (8) airway analyzer: centerline + minimum CSA + stenosis percentage is precisely what this module already computes and validates. Also directly applicable to item (5) carotid encasement (centerline-normal cross-sections give the true perpendicular plane for measuring degrees of circumferential contact) and to difficult-airway assessment.
findings.feasibility: CPU-only, VTK-based, no CUDA. The underlying vmtk/VTK algorithms are reachable from Python; reimplementing MISR-based CSA on SimpleITK/VTK in the FastAPI backend is realistic. Note vmtk itself is often conda-installed — check pip availability on 3.13 or use a 3.11 venv.

findings.title: SlicerJupyter — drive 3D Slicer from a Jupyter kernel
findings.summary: Extension exposing Slicer as a Jupyter kernel using the standard kernel protocol, so the full Slicer Python API (volumes, segmentations, markups, VTK/ITK filters, rendering) is scriptable from notebooks. Related SlicerDocker work supports headless builds and offscreen rendering.
findings.relevance: The practical bridge between Slicer-as-bench and HNRad-as-product: prototype the carotid-encasement, Robbins-level and airway algorithms in a notebook against real cases, capture the numbers as reference values, then port. Also the fastest way to batch-generate ground-truth segmentations for validating item (13).
findings.feasibility: User-level extension install. Headless/offscreen rendering is documented but historically fiddly on Windows without admin — verify.

findings.title: MITK (Medical Imaging Interaction Toolkit) + mitk-python
findings.summary: DKFZ's C++ framework combining ITK + VTK with an application framework, plus the ready-to-use MITK Workbench for viewing, segmentation, registration and multimodal (CT/MRI/PET) overlay with DICOM SEG writing. The v2026.06 release reportedly adds a pip-installable mitk-python package on PyPI and integrates nnInteractive v2.5 and TotalSegmentator v2.14 for AI-assisted segmentation.
findings.relevance: Most permissively licensed of the desktop platforms (BSD-3 beats Slicer for code lifting in some cases). Its interactive segmentation tools and DICOM SEG writer are reference implementations for item (6); the nnInteractive integration is a concrete, already-packaged path for item (13) interactive AI segmentation. mitk-python, if it installs on Windows user-level, would let the FastAPI backend call MITK algorithms directly.
findings.feasibility: Verify mitk-python wheel availability for Python 3.13 on Windows; likely needs a 3.11/3.12 venv. nnInteractive and TotalSegmentator on CPU are minutes-per-case, not seconds — acceptable for a prep-the-night-before workflow, not interactive.

findings.title: Weasis DICOM viewer
findings.summary: Mature Java desktop/web-launched DICOM viewer, v4.7 current with 4.8 in preview. Features listed include 3D & MPR with volume rendering and oblique reconstruction, and DICOM SEG & RT support: SEG overlays in 2D/MPR/3D, RTSTRUCT, RTDOSE isodose and DVH. Supports CT, MR, US, X-ray, PET.
findings.relevance: Best available reference implementation of SEG/RTSTRUCT overlay rendering across 2D, MPR and 3D simultaneously — the exact UX problem in HNRad items (2), (3) and (6). The dual EPL/Apache license makes its rendering and DICOM-parsing logic safe to study and adapt. Also a useful sanity-check viewer to validate HNRad's own SEG output opens correctly elsewhere.
findings.feasibility: Java desktop app; a portable/no-admin distribution exists in principle but is unverified for this workstation. Not a component to embed in a React app — treat as reference plus QA tool.

findings.title: NiiVue — WebGL2 volume/mesh viewer
findings.license: BSD-style (stated on repo; not independently confirmed in this search)
findings.summary: Lightweight WebGL2 browser viewer supporting 30+ volume and mesh formats, running on phone, tablet or desktop. Deliberately exploits WebGL2-only features (non-power-of-two 3D textures, ES 3.0 GLSL, native NIfTI dtype texture formats) for efficient volume handling, with built-in volume rendering and mesh display.
findings.relevance: A much smaller-surface alternative or supplement to Cornerstone3D for HNRad item (3) 3D volume rendering and for displaying STL/mesh output from item (6). Its native-dtype texture approach is a concrete technique to copy if UHD 770 GPU memory becomes the binding constraint. Weaker on DICOM/clinical tooling than Cornerstone3D, so most likely a targeted second viewport rather than a replacement.
findings.feasibility: npm package, WebGL2 only, works on integrated graphics. No CUDA, no server.

findings.title: VTK.js — vtkImageMarchingCubes + vtkSTLWriter in the browser
findings.summary: vtk-js is the JavaScript rewrite of VTK providing WebGL geometry and volume rendering; it includes a working ImageMarchingCubes example (labelmap/image volume to triangle surface) and vtkSTLWriter (https://kitware.github.io/vtk-js/api/IO_Geometry_STLWriter.html) which writes ASCII or binary STL and triangulates non-triangle polygons. WebGPU support exists as preliminary/experimental examples only; volume rendering under WebGPU is not established.
findings.relevance: Completes roadmap item (6) end-to-end entirely client-side: labelmap → marching cubes → smoothing/decimation → binary STL download, with nothing leaving the device and no Python round-trip. Since Cornerstone3D already sits on vtk-js, these classes are in the dependency tree already. Also supports item (9) mandible planner mesh output.
findings.feasibility: Pure JS/WebGL2. Marching cubes on a full-resolution neck CT labelmap will be slow in the main thread — run in a Web Worker and decimate. Do NOT plan on WebGPU volume rendering; treat WebGL2 as the target.

findings.title: VTK WebGPU roadmap discussion (volume rendering timeline)
findings.summary: Kitware's public roadmap thread for WebGPU in the VTK ecosystem. Search-result summaries indicate a 2026 schedule with polydata mapper work and a 2D image mapper earlier in the year and image slice mapping plus volume rendering targeted later (Q3 2026), and a stated intent to move to the official WebGPU C API as it stabilizes. I did not fetch this page directly, so the split between VTK C++ and vtk-js timelines is not confirmed.
findings.relevance: Decides a real architectural question for HNRad item (3): whether to wait for WebGPU volume rendering or ship on WebGL2 now. On this evidence, ship on WebGL2 and treat WebGPU as an opt-in fast path (as OHIF did for GrowCut only).
findings.feasibility: WebGPU availability in a locked-down enterprise Chrome/Edge is itself uncertain on this workstation.

findings.title: highdicom — high-level Python API for standards-compliant DICOM output
findings.summary: Pure-Python layer on pydicom for creating derived DICOM objects: Segmentation (SEG) images, Structured Report documents, Parametric Maps, Key Object Selection documents, Secondary Capture, Grayscale/Color/Pseudo-Color Softcopy Presentation States, Legacy Converted Enhanced CT/PET/MR, and annotations. pip-installable, depends on pydicom + NumPy.
findings.relevance: The correct way to emit HNRad's outputs so they are readable by KP's PACS and by other viewers: SEG for item (6) segmentations, Parametric Map for item (12) SUV maps, SR for item (4) measurements and item (14) reporting, and Presentation States for saved hanging/annotation layouts. Strongly preferred over hand-rolling datasets in pydicom.
findings.feasibility: Pure Python, no compiled deps beyond pydicom/NumPy — the best-case scenario for pip on Python 3.13 user-level with a proxy. Confirm current wheel supports 3.13.

findings.title: Highdicom: a Python Library for Standardized Encoding of Image Annotations and Machine Learning Model Outputs in Pathology and Radiology
findings.venue_or_repo: Journal of Digital Imaging / J Imaging Inform Med
findings.summary: Peer-reviewed description of highdicom's design, demonstrated on slide microscopy and CT, arguing that bridging ML frameworks to DICOM lets developers stay standard-compliant and interoperable with clinical systems at every stage from training to deployment.
findings.relevance: Citable justification for the 'keep everything in DICOM' decision in HNRad's output layer (items 6, 12, 14) — useful when presenting the tool to KP informatics or a tumor board.
findings.feasibility: n/a

findings.title: dcmqi (DICOM for Quantitative Imaging)
findings.summary: C++ library on DCMTK + ITK converting between research formats (NRRD/NIfTI/ITK images) and standard DICOM: itkimage2segimage / segimage2itkimage for SEG, plus parametric map and SR TID1500 measurement conversion. Distributed as precompiled binaries for every major OS, as a Docker image, and as a 3D Slicer extension. Paper: Herz et al., https://aacrjournals.org/cancerres/article/77/21/e87/662591/
findings.relevance: Pragmatic alternative/complement to highdicom for item (6): if the backend works in SimpleITK images (it does), dcmqi's CLI converts a labelmap plus a JSON metadata descriptor into a valid DICOM SEG in one call, including anatomic-region coded concepts — which is exactly what the Robbins neck-level mapper (item 7) needs to encode properly rather than as free text.
findings.feasibility: Precompiled Windows binaries mean no compiler and no admin — just unzip and call from FastAPI via subprocess. Sidesteps any Python 3.13 build problems entirely.

findings.title: rt-utils — minimal Python library for DICOM RTSTRUCT creation/manipulation
findings.summary: pip install rt_utils. Creates a new RTSTRUCT from a DICOM series and adds ROIs from boolean 3D NumPy masks (one 2D plane per slice, ascending slice order), extracts 3D masks back out of existing RTSTRUCT ROIs, sets ROI name/colour/description, and merges two RTSTRUCTs. Companion paper at https://arxiv.org/pdf/2405.06184.
findings.relevance: Contour-based output path for HNRad items (6) and (7): radiation-oncology colleagues and most treatment-planning systems consume RTSTRUCT, not SEG, so emitting both makes HNRad's neck-level and tumour contours immediately usable at tumour board (item 14). Also lets HNRad ingest existing RT contours as priors.
findings.feasibility: Pure Python on pydicom + NumPy; trivial install. Verify Python 3.13 compatibility — the package is small and low-risk to patch if needed.

findings.title: MONAI Label
findings.summary: Server-client AI-in-the-loop annotation framework: a Python server exposes inference/training endpoints, and client plugins exist for 3D Slicer, OHIF/Cornerstone3D, MITK, QuPath, CVAT. Implements DeepEdit/DeepGrow interactive paradigms plus active learning (suggests the next volume to label and retrains from user corrections). Sample radiology apps include DeepEdit, DeepGrow, generic segmentation, multi-stage vertebra segmentation, and MONAI bundles such as whole-body segmentation and tumour segmentation. Python >= 3.10 for the default SAM-2 inclusion.
findings.relevance: The reference architecture for HNRad item (13): a local FastAPI-style AI server that an OHIF/Cornerstone3D front end talks to over HTTP — the same topology HNRad already has. The existing OHIF plugin means the client-side protocol is already written and MIT/Apache licensed. Active learning is the realistic path to an H&N-specific model built from the surgeon's own corrected cases, all on-device.
findings.feasibility: Documentation and dependencies assume CUDA; CPU-only inference is not explicitly supported and will be slow for 3D models. Python >= 3.10 but 3.13 support is unverified — plan a separate 3.11 venv. Borrow the protocol and client plugin even if you do not run the MONAI server itself.

findings.title: MONAI Label: A framework for AI-assisted interactive labeling of 3D medical images
findings.summary: Peer-reviewed description of the MONAI Label framework, its interactive annotation paradigms (DeepEdit, DeepGrow), active-learning strategies and viewer integrations. Abstract only was retrieved (paywalled on ScienceDirect).
findings.relevance: Evidence base for the claim that AI-in-the-loop annotation materially reduces labelling effort — the justification for building item (13) as interactive-assist rather than fully automatic, which is also the safer clinical posture for a surgical planning tool.
findings.feasibility: n/a

findings.title: Orthanc — lightweight standalone DICOM server with DICOMweb
findings.summary: Single-binary RESTful DICOM server needing no external database or dependencies, extensible via a REST API and a plugin mechanism (web viewer, PostgreSQL/MySQL back-ends, Python plugin, and an official DICOMweb plugin implementing WADO-URI, WADO-RS, QIDO-RS and STOW-RS per PS3.18). Windows ships in two forms: a service installer, and a command-line build you extract into a folder and run manually. Ecosystem paper: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5959835/
findings.relevance: The obvious backend for roadmap item (1) local DICOM library: it gives HNRad a real DICOMweb endpoint, which is exactly what Cornerstone3D/OHIF expect, instead of a bespoke file-walker. QIDO-RS gives study/series search for free; STOW-RS gives a place to store SEG/RTSTRUCT written back by items (6) and (7).
findings.feasibility: The command-line Windows build runs from a user folder with no service registration and no admin — the key fact for this workstation. Everything stays on localhost. LICENSE CAUTION: GPLv3 core and AGPL DICOMweb plugin. Running Orthanc as a separate localhost process that HNRad talks to over HTTP keeps HNRad's own code out of the copyleft boundary; do not statically link or vendor it.

findings.title: dcm4chee-arc-light (DCM4CHE Archive 5)
findings.license: MPL 1.1 / GPL / LGPL tri-license (per dcm4che project; not confirmed in this search)
findings.summary: Full-featured open-source PACS / vendor-neutral archive: Java EE application on WildFly requiring JDK 17+, with LDAP as central configuration per the DICOM Application Configuration Management Profile, broad DICOM service and transfer-syntax support, and DICOMweb.
findings.relevance: Reference for what a production archive's DICOMweb and query model look like, and a comparison point when designing item (1). Not a fit for HNRad itself.
findings.feasibility: Requires JDK 17+, WildFly and an LDAP directory — far too heavy for a no-admin single workstation. Use Orthanc instead.

findings.title: Kaapana — open-source platform for integrating AI in medical imaging research
findings.summary: DKFZ toolkit for provisioning medical-imaging analysis platforms: DICOM ingestion, cohort curation, Airflow-style workflow orchestration, researcher-facing apps and result inspection under one UI, plus federated/distributed scenarios. Deployed across RACOON (38 German university clinics), the DKTK Joint Imaging Platform (11 clinics) and Cancer Core Europe DART (7 centres). Paper: Akünal, Bujotzek, Denner, Nolden, Neher, Floca, Maier-Hein et al., arXiv:2512.09644 (Dec 2025), https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.09644
findings.relevance: Not deployable here, but the most thoroughly documented answer to 'how do you wire a DICOM store, a cohort browser, a workflow engine and a viewer into one coherent product' — worth reading for HNRad's item (1)+(14) data/workflow model. Its 'bring the algorithm to the data' framing is also the exact argument for HNRad being local-only.
findings.feasibility: Requires Kubernetes (single VM minimum, realistically a cluster) — impossible on a locked-down Win11 workstation with no admin. AGPL-3.0 makes code reuse in a closed tool problematic.

gaps: Could not confirm whether 3D Slicer, Weasis or MITK Workbench install and run on Windows 11 without administrator rights — all three appear to offer archive/portable distributions but I found no authoritative statement. This needs to be tested on the actual workstation.

Could not confirm the VTK.js (as opposed to VTK C++) WebGPU volume-rendering timeline; the roadmap page at discourse.vtk.org was not fetched directly and the search summary may conflate the two projects.
Could not confirm whether highdicom, rt-utils, dcmqi's Python wrapper, or mitk-python publish wheels compatible with Python 3.13 on Windows — each may force a separate 3.11 venv.

Could not confirm the actual MAX_3D_TEXTURE_SIZE / MAX_TEXTURE_SIZE reported by the Intel UHD 770 driver in the enterprise browser build, nor whether WebGPU is enabled — both are decisive for roadmap items (2), (3) and (6) and should be measured first.

Web search budget was exhausted mid-task, so I could not cover: OHIF's TMTV/PET-SUV mode in detail (only its existence is confirmed from the OHIF README), OHIF's local-file datasource for fully offline use, ITK-SNAP, Starviewer, the @cornerstonejs/ai package internals, or Cornerstone3D's surface/contour segmentation representation maturity.
No head-and-neck-specific OHIF extension, Slicer extension or hanging protocol was found; if one exists it did not surface in these searches.
dcm4chee's exact license text was not verified (stated tri-license is from general knowledge, not a retrieved source).
sweeps.topic: viewers-platforms: open-source medical imaging viewers, DICOM servers and platforms relevant to HNRad
Clinical validation, regulatory status and deployment lessons for AI in head & neck radiology — applied to HNRad (local-only H&N surgical radiology assistant)

findings.title: FUTURE-AI: international consensus guideline for trustworthy and deployable artificial intelligence in healthcare
findings.summary: Consensus guideline from 117 experts in 50 countries. Six principles — Fairness, Universality, Traceability, Usability, Robustness, Explainability — operationalised as 30 best practices spanning design, development, validation, regulation, deployment and monitoring, with medical-imaging-specific instantiations. Traceability explicitly covers logging of AI outputs, user actions and version history after deployment.
findings.relevance: The single best scaffold for HNRad's whole quality story. 'Traceability' maps directly onto the audit-logging requirement; 'Usability' and 'Robustness' onto roadmap items 5-13 (encasement degrees, segmentation, ENE/HPV). Use it as the checklist that HNRad's design doc is written against.
findings.feasibility: n/a (process guidance); no compute cost

findings.title: A joint ESTRO and AAPM guideline for development, clinical validation and reporting of artificial intelligence models in radiation therapy
findings.summary: Delphi-derived guideline covering image analysis, volume segmentation, treatment planning, QA, adaptive workflows, outcome prediction and the training/validation/testing of AI models. Emphasises model availability, transparency and standardised reporting so results are reproducible enough to support clinical integration. Notes EU AI Act classifies medical-device AI as high-risk.
findings.relevance: The closest thing to a domain-specific SOP for HNRad's AI organ segmentation (item 13) and any predictive model (ENE, HPV). Its segmentation and validation sections give a defensible test protocol for a single-operator, in-house tool.
findings.feasibility: n/a (process guidance)
findings.license: Journal-published guideline; text may be paywalled

findings.title: Metrics reloaded: recommendations for image analysis validation
findings.summary: Large Delphi consortium framework for problem-aware metric selection using a 'problem fingerprint'. Shows that Dice alone is misleading for small, tubular or boundary-critical structures and recommends boundary metrics (NSD, HD95) and detection metrics where appropriate. Reference implementations released in MONAI.
findings.relevance: Tells HNRad which numbers to report for carotid encasement (item 5), airway CSA (item 8), mandibular canal (item 9) and volumetrics (item 6). Tubular/thin structures are exactly the pitfall class it warns about. The Python package is a usable dependency.
findings.feasibility: Pure-Python/NumPy metric library, CPU-only, pip-installable; MONAI ecosystem may need a 3.11 venv on Windows — metrics themselves are lightweight

findings.title: Clinically Applicable Segmentation of Head and Neck Anatomy for Radiotherapy: Deep Learning Algorithm Development and Validation Study
findings.venue_or_repo: J Med Internet Res 23(7):e26151 (DeepMind / UCLH; DOI 10.2196/26151)
findings.summary: Seminal H&N OAR segmentation study on 663 routine CT scans. Introduced the surface Dice similarity coefficient (surface DSC), which measures deviation of organ surfaces within a clinically derived tolerance rather than volume overlap, because it correlates with how much boundary a human must actually redraw.
findings.relevance: Surface DSC is the right acceptance metric for HNRad's segmentation (item 6) and neck-level mapper (item 7): it quantifies editing burden, not overlap. Also establishes the per-organ tolerance-band idea HNRad can reuse when defining 'accept vs edit' thresholds.
findings.feasibility: n/a for the model (not released for clinical use); surface DSC is trivially implementable with SimpleITK/scikit-image on CPU
findings.license: Paper CC BY; model weights not openly licensed for clinical use

findings.title: Multicentre evaluation of deep learning CT autosegmentation of the head and neck region for radiotherapy (HARMONY study)
findings.summary: Seven centres on four continents, two phases, 11 nodal levels plus 7 OARs (MVision software). Time savings 42% then 49%; but levels IA, IB, III, IVA, IVB showed no significant saving and some centres edited longer than manual. All edited contours reduced inter-observer variability. Excluded post-operative cases and dental-artefact scans.
findings.relevance: Directly benchmarks HNRad's Robbins neck-level mapper (item 7). The headline lesson: nodal levels are where autosegmentation fails to pay off, and post-op necks and dental artefact were excluded — precisely HNRad's surgical population. Sets realistic expectations and a validation design to copy.
findings.feasibility: n/a

findings.title: Real-world performance evaluation of commercial autocontouring software for head and neck cancer radiotherapy (ART-Plan / Therapanacea)
findings.summary: Retrospective (n=60) plus prospective (n=61) NICE-style evaluation. Median volumetric Dice ranged 0.23-0.88 across structures; blinded preference was ~even between AI and clinician contours. Significant review/edit time saving for all structures, but clinically significant dosimetric differences persisted for larynx and elective nodal volumes despite good geometry.
findings.relevance: Model evaluation design for HNRad: pair geometric metrics with a blinded clinician-preference test and a downstream-impact test. Shows a structure can look geometrically fine and still be clinically wrong — a warning for HNRad's encasement degrees and airway metrics where a small boundary error changes the number reported.
findings.feasibility: n/a

findings.title: Using Failure Mode and Effects Analysis to Evaluate Risk in the Clinical Adoption of Automated Contouring and Treatment Planning Tools
findings.summary: FMEA of MD Anderson's Radiation Planning Assistant found 126 failure modes unique to the automated workflow out of 290 possible; mean RPN 56.3, max 486. The top 10 were driven by automation bias, operator error and software error. Twenty-one exceeded the action threshold; UI simplification and training cut mean RPN to 33.7.
findings.relevance: A ready-made risk-analysis template for HNRad. Because HNRad is single-developer and single-user, automation bias is the dominant hazard: the surgeon who built it is the surgeon who trusts it. Recommend running this FMEA before item 13 (AI segmentation) ships, and designing the UI to force explicit review.
findings.feasibility: n/a (risk process; a half-day exercise)

findings.title: Monitoring Variations in the Use of Automated Contouring Software
findings.summary: 500 head-and-neck patients contoured by an in-house automated system. Dice and added path length between auto and final contours were tracked on statistical process control charts with 3-SD limits. Major-edit rates: optic nerve 11%/6.1%, parotid 5.9%, oesophagus 4.8%, mandible 2.5%. Moving-mean charts flagged individual users whose editing declined over time — a measurable automation-bias signal.
findings.relevance: This is the concrete design for HNRad's audit log. Store the AI mask and the surgeon's final mask, compute Dice + added path length per structure per case, and chart them over time. Decreasing edit magnitude is the drift/automation-bias alarm. All computable locally with SimpleITK/scikit-image.
findings.feasibility: Fully CPU/offline: added path length and Dice are cheap; SPC charts are a few lines of NumPy. Fits the FastAPI backend as a background job
findings.license: Journal article (Elsevier); the method is free to reimplement

findings.title: Human factors in the clinical implementation of deep learning-based automated contouring of pelvic organs at risk for MRI-guided radiotherapy
findings.summary: Deployed a UNet for 0.35T MR pelvic OARs and studied the human side: fraction of slices left unmodified, blinded clinical-significance grading of residual deviations, and a pre/post experiment comparing clinically used contours with three-expert consensus. Objectively measured whether auto-contouring pulled final contours toward or away from an independent standard.
findings.relevance: The methodological answer to 'did the tool make me better or just faster?'. HNRad should run the same pre/post consensus comparison before trusting AI segmentation for volumetrics or STL export (items 6, 9) — otherwise time saved is indistinguishable from accuracy lost.
findings.feasibility: n/a (study design; needs a second reader for consensus, which is the main practical constraint for a solo user)

findings.title: Point/Counterpoint: Extensive upfront validation and testing are needed prior to the clinical implementation of AI-based auto-segmentation tools
findings.venue_or_repo: J Appl Clin Med Phys 24:e13873 (DOI 10.1002/acm2.13873, PMID 36545883)
findings.summary: Roper argues for 400+ case multi-site testing with slice-by-slice visual review, citing gross failures (lumbar spine contoured as bladder) and subtle ones (missing spinal cord segments) that geometric metrics miss. Lin argues small targeted samples plus continuous post-implementation monitoring, automatic contour-integrity checks and tracking of inferior cases. Both agree human review remains mandatory.
findings.relevance: Settles HNRad's validation budget question realistically: a solo developer cannot do 400 cases, so adopt Lin's position — small targeted test set plus automated contour-integrity checks (connected components, expected volume/laterality ranges, topology) that run on every case. Cheap to implement in scikit-image.
findings.feasibility: Integrity checks are trivial CPU-side (SimpleITK connected-component + volume/laterality sanity rules)

findings.title: ACR-SIIM Practice Parameter for Imaging Artificial Intelligence (first imaging-AI practice parameter)
findings.summary: Approved at ACR 2026. Sets out how a practice should govern imaging AI: form a governance group, maintain an inventory of tools and versions, run local acceptance testing before deployment, monitor real-world performance for drift and safety, define stop rules, and address privacy and bias. Pairs with the Assess-AI framework.
findings.relevance: The US professional-standard answer to 'what must a site do before using AI on real patients'. HNRad, as an in-house tool at Kaiser, should satisfy this even though it is not a marketed device: version inventory, local acceptance test record, stop rules. Directly shapes the reporting/export module (item 14).
findings.feasibility: n/a (governance)
findings.license: ACR practice parameter (free preview via ACR Gravitas)

findings.title: ACR Assess-AI national AI quality registry and ARCH-AI recognition program
findings.venue_or_repo: J Am Coll Radiol (DOI 10.1016/j.jacr.2026.04.024, PMID 42066927); program page https://www.acr.org/News-and-Publications/Responsible-Artificial-Intelligence-in-Radiology
findings.summary: Assess-AI ingests de-identified AI output, report text and DICOM metadata via ACR Connect, derives surrogate labels from reports with LLM pipelines, and returns concordance dashboards benchmarked against peers; a local Forensics App re-identifies discordant cases. ARCH-AI (launched June 2024) recognises sites doing this; 22 health systems / 965 facilities enrolled.
findings.relevance: Shows the reference architecture for post-deployment monitoring — and its local-adjudication pattern (central metrics, local re-identification) is the model HNRad should copy entirely on-device. HNRad cannot and must not send data out, so build the dashboard locally; note that participation is not an option for a nothing-leaves-the-device tool.
findings.feasibility: Registry participation is off the table (data egress). The local-dashboard pattern is fully implementable in FastAPI + React
findings.license: ACR program; registry participation is fee/enrollment-based

findings.title: NICE HTE11: Artificial intelligence technologies to aid contouring for radiotherapy treatment planning — early value assessment
findings.venue_or_repo: National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (UK)
findings.summary: Conditionally recommends nine AI auto-contouring technologies (including MVision Segmentation Service, >160 structures, and RayStation, >70 CT structures) for NHS use while further evidence is generated, always with radiation-oncology professional review. Publishes an evidence-generation plan proposing before/after studies at implementing departments.
findings.relevance: Two things HNRad can lift: (1) the canonical list of currently-accepted commercial contouring products to benchmark against, and (2) NICE's before/after evidence-generation design, which is the most feasible study a single surgeon could actually run on their own cases (time, edit magnitude, plan/decision change).
findings.feasibility: n/a

findings.title: RCR guidance on auto-contouring in radiotherapy (Clinical Oncology)
findings.summary: Professional-body guidance on introducing auto-contouring: commissioning/acceptance testing, ongoing QA, mandatory human review, documentation and staff training. I retrieved and downloaded the PDF (URL confirmed live, ~1.1 MB) but could not extract its text in this environment, so the specific recommendations above come from the search-result title and snippet rather than the document body.
findings.relevance: UK counterpart to the ACR-SIIM parameter; worth reading in full for the commissioning checklist and the explicit statement that auto-contours are a starting point requiring clinician review — the governance framing HNRad needs for any surgeon-facing AI output.
findings.feasibility: n/a

findings.title: FDA Clinical Decision Support Software guidance (final 2022; revised final issued January 2026)
findings.summary: Interprets the 21st Century Cures Act four-criteria test for Non-Device CDS. Critically, software that acquires, processes or analyses a medical image fails criterion 1 — so image-analysis software (segmentation, measurement, pattern recognition on radiological images) is a device and cannot use the CDS exemption. A revised final guidance dated 6 Jan 2026 supersedes the 2022 version.
findings.relevance: The decisive regulatory fact for HNRad. Everything HNRad does — segmentation, encasement degrees, min CSA, SUV/MTV — is image analysis, so it would be a regulated device if it were distributed. That is an argument for keeping it strictly local, unmarketed, research/personal-practice use, and for documenting that intent explicitly.
findings.feasibility: n/a — but shapes whether HNRad may ever be shared with colleagues

findings.title: MDCG 2023-1: Guidance on the health institution exemption under Article 5(5) of EU MDR/IVDR (in-house devices)
findings.venue_or_repo: European Commission / Medical Device Coordination Group
findings.summary: Lets EU health institutions manufacture, modify and use in-house devices without CE marking, provided the device is made and used only within that institution, meets a need no equivalent CE-marked device meets, and is backed by a documented quality system, design justification, and information supplied to the competent authority on request.
findings.relevance: There is no clean US equivalent, but this is the best-articulated template for what an in-house clinical software tool must document: design rationale, why no commercial product suffices, QMS, and use confined to the institution. A useful model for the governance file HNRad should keep even in a US/Kaiser context.
findings.feasibility: n/a; EU-only in force, used here as a documentation template

findings.title: FDA/Health Canada/MHRA Good Machine Learning Practice (10 principles), Transparency principles, and Predetermined Change Control Plan guiding principles
findings.summary: Ten GMLP principles (2021) including Principle 10: deployed models are monitored for performance and retraining risk is managed. A later transparency set requires users be told subgroup performance, training/test data characteristics, and modifications from real-world monitoring. Five joint PCCP principles define how a model may be updated post-authorisation without new review.
findings.relevance: Gives HNRad a model-card contract: for every AI model shipped inside the app, record training data, subgroup performance, version, and monitoring plan, and surface it in the UI. The PCCP concept is the discipline to adopt if HNRad ever swaps in a retrained segmentation model — change control, not silent replacement.
findings.feasibility: n/a (documentation practice); a model-card JSON per bundled model is trivial

findings.title: Navigating the intersection of 3D printing, software regulation and quality control for point-of-care manufacturing of personalized anatomical models
findings.summary: Reviews FDA's stance on software used to produce 3D-printed anatomical models and compiles, for the first time, the list of cleared software platforms (e.g. Materialise Mimics inPrint, Synopsys Simpleware ScanIP Medical, 3D Systems D2P) with the printers validated against each. Also covers verification/validation, sources of model inaccuracy, and accuracy-testing standards.
findings.relevance: Essential for HNRad's STL export and mandible planner (items 6 and 9). It establishes that models intended for diagnostic or surgical-planning use are expected to come from cleared segmentation software, and it gives the accuracy-verification methods HNRad must implement (phantom/known-geometry checks) if it exports STLs from its own pipeline.
findings.feasibility: Accuracy verification via a printed/known phantom is CPU-only and cheap; the regulatory point constrains how HNRad's STLs may be labelled and used

findings.title: MIM Contour ProtégéAI / ProtégéAI+ 2.0 — FDA 510(k) clearances including on-premise local deployment
findings.summary: MIM obtained 510(k) clearance for additional AI contours (head and neck, thorax, prostate, abdomen) explicitly together with local, on-premise deployment rather than cloud inference. The later GE HealthCare ProtégéAI+ 2.0 clearance extends contours and automates initiation with minimal user interaction, processing CT and MR and exporting to treatment planning systems.
findings.relevance: Precedent that a fully on-premise, no-egress AI contouring deployment is a cleared, commercially normal configuration — useful when justifying HNRad's local-only architecture to IT or compliance at Kaiser. Also a functional benchmark for item 13.
findings.feasibility: Commercial product, not adoptable for HNRad; cited as architectural precedent

findings.title: MVision AI Contour+ — FDA 510(k) clearance for advanced CT and MR models
findings.summary: Contour+ cleared for additional CT and MR models; the product now covers 159 organs-at-risk and 67 lymph node regions in the US market. This is the same vendor whose H&N model was independently evaluated across seven institutions in the HARMONY npj Digital Medicine study.
findings.relevance: The de facto benchmark for how many H&N structures a mature tool covers, and the only one with published seven-centre independent H&N nodal-level data. Useful as the comparator when scoping HNRad's Robbins neck-level mapper (item 7) — note the independent study found nodal levels were where it saved no time.
findings.feasibility: Commercial, cloud/on-prem service; not adoptable locally

findings.title: Pretreatment CT Identification of Extranodal Extension in Laryngeal and Hypopharyngeal Cancers Using Deep Learning (DeepENE)
findings.summary: 289 patients, 1954 pathologically confirmed nodes from Fudan; internal AUC 0.93 for ENE, external AUCs 0.96, 0.87 and 0.90 across three external LHSCC cohorts plus an oral SCC cohort. Outperformed five board-certified head and neck specialists. Retrospective; node-level reference standard from pathology.
findings.relevance: The strongest externally validated ENE evidence to date and the right accuracy bar for any ENE feature in HNRad. Note the drop from 0.96 to 0.87 across sites — direct evidence that HNRad must locally validate any borrowed ENE model on Kaiser scans before showing a number to a surgeon.
findings.feasibility: Weights not stated as released; if obtained, node-level CNN inference on cropped ROIs is CPU-feasible. Assume re-implementation rather than reuse
findings.license: Not stated in retrieved material — treat as research-only until confirmed

findings.title: Artificial Intelligence Model for Imaging-Based Extranodal Extension Detection and Outcome Prediction in HPV-Positive Oropharyngeal Cancer
findings.venue_or_repo: JAMA Otolaryngol Head Neck Surg (DOI 10.1001/jamaoto.2025.3225, PMID 41026592)
findings.summary: Single-centre Montreal cohort of HPV-positive cN+ OPC treated with upfront (chemo)radiotherapy 2009-2020. nnU-Net for nodal segmentation, then radiomic vs deep features for iENE classification, benchmarked against two expert neuroradiologists by AUC and linked to OS, RFS, distant control and locoregional control.
findings.relevance: Shows the full pipeline HNRad would need for imaging-based ENE: nnU-Net node segmentation then classification, with outcome linkage rather than just AUC. nnU-Net is openly licensed and CPU-runnable, making this the most reproducible ENE architecture for a local build. Single-centre, no external validation — treat as a design template, not a validated claim.
findings.feasibility: nnU-Net inference runs on CPU (slow: minutes per case on a UHD 770 box, no CUDA needed); nnU-Net requires a Python 3.11 venv in practice on Windows
findings.license: Paper subscription; nnU-Net itself is Apache-2.0

findings.title: Systematic review of artificial intelligence and radiomics for preoperative prediction of extranodal extension and lymph node metastasis in oropharyngeal cancer
findings.summary: PRISMA review of 11 studies (2020-2025), risk of bias by PROBAST and reporting quality by TRIPOD. Task-specific DL ENE model reached AUC 0.86 with usable operating points; a generalist vision-language model reached sensitivity 1.00 but specificity 0.34. Decision-curve analysis favoured the DL model, quantifying fewer unnecessary neck dissections per 1000 patients. Only one LNM study had external validation.
findings.relevance: Two lessons for HNRad. First, report decision-curve / per-1000-patients impact, not just AUC — that is the number a surgeon can act on. Second, the field's external-validation record is thin, so any ENE/HPV feature in HNRad should be labelled investigational in the UI and the reporting export (item 14).
findings.feasibility: n/a

findings.title: TRIPOD+AI statement: updated guidance for reporting clinical prediction models that use regression or machine learning methods
findings.summary: 27-item checklist superseding TRIPOD 2015, harmonising reporting for prediction models whether built by regression or machine learning, with a separate abstracts checklist. Covers data sources, participants, predictors, sample size, missing data, model specification, performance measures including calibration, and fairness.
findings.relevance: The checklist for HNRad's non-segmentation predictors — ENE risk, HPV status, difficult-airway flags. Its insistence on calibration (not just discrimination) matters: a surgeon acting on a probability needs it to be calibrated, and the ENE literature above frequently omits this.
findings.feasibility: n/a

findings.title: DECIDE-AI: a new reporting guideline and its relevance to artificial intelligence studies in radiology
findings.summary: Radiology-facing explainer of DECIDE-AI, a stage-specific reporting guideline for the early, live clinical evaluation of AI decision-support systems. It fills the gap between offline algorithm validation (TRIPOD+AI/CLAIM) and full trials (SPIRIT-AI/CONSORT-AI) by demanding reporting of human factors, user interaction and implementation context.
findings.relevance: This is exactly HNRad's evaluation stage: one clinician, live cases, small n, human factors dominant. DECIDE-AI defines what to record during that first-in-practice period — interaction data, errors, near-misses, user trust — which doubles as the specification for HNRad's audit log and any future write-up.
findings.feasibility: n/a
findings.license: Journal article (Elsevier); the DECIDE-AI checklist itself is freely available via EQUATOR

findings.title: A comprehensive multifaceted technical evaluation framework for implementation of auto-segmentation models in radiotherapy
findings.summary: Proposes an end-to-end technical evaluation framework for commissioning auto-segmentation models before clinical release, spanning geometric, dosimetric and workflow dimensions. I confirmed the article exists at this Nature URL via search, but the publisher redirected authentication and I could not read the full text, so the specific tests, metrics and any code/licence terms are unverified.
findings.relevance: Likely the most directly reusable commissioning protocol for HNRad's AI segmentation step (item 13) — worth retrieving in full. Flagged rather than adopted because I could not confirm its contents.
findings.feasibility: Unknown; open-access Nature journal so full text should be retrievable via PMC
findings.license: Communications Medicine is open access (likely CC BY) — unconfirmed

gaps: The CLAIM checklist (Checklist for AI in Medical Imaging) and its 2024 update in Radiology: Artificial Intelligence — I found 62 PubMed hits for the topic but did not retrieve a confirmed canonical URL/DOI for the CLAIM 2024 update, so I deliberately omitted it rather than cite an unverified link. It should be added; it is the imaging-specific counterpart to TRIPOD+AI.
