No published prospective study or RCT of AI segmentation used for head & neck SURGICAL planning (as opposed to radiotherapy contouring) was found. Essentially all clinical validation evidence for H&N autosegmentation comes from radiation oncology, where the downstream endpoint is dose, not an osteotomy or a decision to resect the carotid. HNRad's core use case has no validation literature of its own.

I could not find validation studies specific to HNRad's distinctive analytics: carotid encasement degree measurement, airway minimum cross-sectional area / stenosis quantification, mandibular canal localisation accuracy, or automated Robbins level assignment in POST-OPERATIVE necks. The HARMONY multicentre study explicitly excluded post-operative cases and dental-artefact scans, which is the population HNRad serves.

No literature found on audit-logging design, provenance or version control specifically for offline/air-gapped clinical imaging software. The Assess-AI and SPC-monitoring papers provide the closest analogues but both assume a networked, multi-user institutional deployment.

Could not extract the text of the RCR 2024 auto-contouring guidance (PDF downloaded, no PDF text extraction available in this environment) or the Communications Medicine 2025 evaluation framework (publisher auth redirect). Both should be re-fetched.

WebSearch budget for the session was exhausted before I could search FDA clearance requirements for virtual surgical planning / mandible reconstruction software specifically (Materialise, 3D Systems VSP), RSNA 3D Printing SIG quality-assurance guidelines for anatomic models, or validated open-source mandible/fibula segmentation code. The Paxton 3D Print Med review partially covers the software-clearance question.

No information retrieved on Kaiser Permanente's own internal governance requirements for clinician-developed clinical software, which would be the binding constraint in practice regardless of FDA status.

sweeps.topic: foundation-vlm: CT foundation models and vision-language models for radiology, judged for local CPU-only deployment in HNRad (head & neck surgical radiology assistant)

findings.title: CT-FM: self-supervised 3D CT foundation model (SegResEncoder, 77M params)
findings.summary: Pretrained with modified SimCLR on 148,000 CT scans; convolutional SegResEncoder vision backbone with 77M parameters. Reported whole-body segmentation mean Dice 0.898 over 117 labels, head-CT triage F1 0.776 (SinoCT) and 0.754 (CQ500), plus strong anatomical/lesion image retrieval and semantic clustering. MIT licensed; integrates with MONAI Auto3DSeg and project-lighter pipelines.
findings.relevance: Best CPU candidate for roadmap items 6 (segmentation/volumetrics), 13 (AI organ segmentation) and as a generic feature extractor for 5/7/12. A 77M CNN encoder is the only class of CT foundation model realistically runnable on an Intel UHD 770 box; embeddings can be cached once per study and reused by downstream linear heads.
findings.feasibility: 77M-param CNN -> roughly 300MB fp32; PyTorch CPU inference on a 512x512x300 CT is minutes, not hours, with patch-based sliding window. MONAI/lighter pin older torch; build a separate Python 3.11 venv rather than fighting 3.13 wheels. No CUDA required.

findings.title: Merlin: a 3D CT vision-language foundation model (Stanford MIMI)
findings.venue_or_repo: arXiv 2406.06512 / Nature 2026 per model card; github.com/StanfordMIMI/Merlin; huggingface.co/stanfordmimi/Merlin
findings.summary: 3D VLM trained on >6M images from 15,331 abdominal CTs paired with >1.8M ICD codes and >6M report tokens. Evaluated on 6 task types and 752 individual tasks (30-finding zero-shot classification, 692 phenotypes, cross-modal retrieval, 5-year disease prediction, report generation, 20-organ segmentation), internal 5,137 scans, external 44,098 scans across 3 sites plus 2 public datasets. MIT license, pip install merlin-vlm.
findings.relevance: The reference architecture for what HNRad could eventually be: a local CT encoder producing embeddings plus optional phenotype/report heads (roadmap 13, 14). MIT license and a real pip package make it the most legally clean VLM here. Caveat: pretraining is abdominal CT, so neck anatomy is out-of-distribution.
findings.feasibility: pip installable, but the repo documents no CPU path and no parameter count; image encoder is 3D and memory-hungry. Expect to run embedding extraction only, batch size 1, and budget several GB RAM per volume. Test on a neck CT before assuming any transfer.

findings.title: CT-CLIP / CT-RATE / CT-CHAT: generalist foundation models from a multimodal 3D CT dataset
findings.venue_or_repo: arXiv 2403.17834; github.com/ibrahimethemhamamci/CT-CLIP; CT-RATE on Hugging Face
findings.summary: CT-RATE pairs 25,692 non-contrast chest CTs from 21,304 patients (expanded to 50,188 volumes) with reports. CT-CLIP is the contrastive vision-language model; CT-CHAT the chat VLM. Repo states A100 80GB for training batch size 8; inference ~1.5s per volume for 18 pathologies zero-shot, 0.5s with ClassFine, on GPU. Everything (models and dataset) is CC-BY-NC-SA.
findings.relevance: The de-facto benchmark substrate for 3D CT VLM work — nearly every paper below reports on CT-RATE. Useful as a reference for how to structure HNRad's own local report/label pipeline (roadmap 14), but the non-commercial share-alike license and chest-only scope limit direct reuse.
findings.license: CC-BY-NC-SA 4.0 (non-commercial, share-alike) — flag clearly; not Apache/MIT
findings.feasibility: No CPU inference documented. Repo assumes CUDA; patch-size reduction is the only documented downscaling path. Treat as a source of ideas and eval data, not as a local runtime.

findings.title: MedGemma 1.5 4B — Gemma-3-based medical VLM with 3D CT/MRI volume support
findings.venue_or_repo: Hugging Face google/medgemma-1.5-4b-it; technical report arXiv 2604.05081
findings.summary: 4B-parameter medical VLM. Version 1.5 adds interpretation of 3D volume representations of CT and MRI, histopathology, and multi-timepoint analysis; reports 11% improvement in 3D MRI condition classification and 47% macro-F1 gain in pathology over v1. Model card warns it has not been evaluated for multi-turn use or multi-image comprehension, is prompt-sensitive relative to Gemma 3, and outputs are not intended to inform diagnosis without fine-tuning and validation.
findings.relevance: The only mainstream small VLM that officially claims 3D CT input, which maps onto roadmap 14 (reporting / tumor board export) and possibly narrative summarization of measurements HNRad already computes. Safer framing: let HNRad compute the numbers deterministically and use the VLM only to phrase them.
findings.license: Health AI Developer Foundations terms of use (gated on Hugging Face; NOT Apache/MIT — review before any deployment)
findings.feasibility: Quantized builds exist for llama.cpp, Ollama, LM Studio and Jan; Ollama lists medgemma:4b at 3.3GB, which fits 32GB RAM comfortably. Expect low single-digit tokens/sec on CPU with no CUDA. Model card explicitly recommends GPU and says CPU is not recommended for clinical use. Volumetric input needs preprocessing code from the Google repo.

findings.title: MedGemma technical report (4B and 27B)
findings.summary: Gemma-3-derived medical models at 4B and 27B parameters; reports 2.6-10% improvement on medical multimodal question answering and 15.5-18.1% improvement on chest X-ray finding classification versus base Gemma 3. Trained on chest X-ray, pathology, dermatology and fundus images; the original 4B card does not claim CT or 3D support (that arrives in 1.5).
findings.relevance: Baseline context for roadmap 14. Important negative: the v1 model was never trained on CT, so any H&N CT performance claim from v1 would be unfounded.
findings.license: Health AI Developer Foundations terms of use
findings.feasibility: 4B quantized runs on CPU; 27B (17GB in Ollama) would fit 32GB RAM but be impractically slow without a GPU.

findings.title: Pillar-0: a new frontier for radiology foundation models
findings.summary: Pretrained on 42,990 abdomen-pelvis CTs, 86,411 chest CTs, 14,348 head CTs and 11,543 breast MRIs, with a RATE framework using LLMs to extract structured labels for 366 radiologic findings. Mean AUROC 86.4 (abdomen-pelvis), 88.0 (chest), 90.1 (head), 82.9 (breast); reported to outperform MedGemma, MedImageInsight, Lingshu and Merlin by 7.8-15.8 AUROC points. Preserves grayscale contrast instead of downsampling volumes to low-resolution 2D slices.
findings.relevance: Strongest published evidence that full-resolution volumetric processing (not slice downsampling) is what makes CT foundation models work — a direct design lesson for how HNRad should feed neck CTs to any encoder. Head CT pretraining is the closest existing corpus to H&N anatomy.
findings.license: Paper posted CC-BY-NC-SA 4.0; weights/code availability not confirmed from the abstract page — treat licensing as unknown
findings.feasibility: No code repo confirmed (a github.com/reginabarzilaygroup/Pillar-0 fetch returned 404). Architecture and parameter count not stated on the abstract page. Cannot assess CPU feasibility yet.

findings.title: Empirical investigation of 3D CT foundation models and unsupervised adaptation for head and neck cancer recurrence prediction
findings.summary: Benchmarks multiple 3D CT foundation models for recurrence-free survival across two public datasets totalling 3,644 H&N cancer patients. Finds persistent difficulty identifying features that generalize across imaging distributions, with significant performance drops on external validation. Concludes that combining imaging features with clinical data remains the most accurate approach.
findings.relevance: The single most directly on-topic paper for HNRad: it is H&N, it is CT, and it is a foundation-model benchmark. The headline message is a caution — do not ship a foundation-model prognostic score (ENE, HPV, recurrence) without external validation, because these embeddings do not transfer across scanners/sites.
findings.feasibility: n/a — methodological evidence, not code to deploy.

findings.title: Comparing foundation model derived embeddings with traditional approaches for distant metastasis prediction in head and neck cancer
findings.summary: Uses 2,327 RADCURE patients. CT Foundation-derived embeddings achieved AUC 0.791 for distant metastasis risk, beating radiomics (0.772) and conventional deep learning (0.753), with minimal preprocessing and no hand-engineered feature design.
findings.relevance: Evidence that frozen CT-foundation embeddings plus a small classifier is a viable, low-effort route to H&N risk scores — exactly the CPU-friendly pattern HNRad can afford (encode once, train a logistic/GBM head locally). Gains over radiomics are real but modest (~0.02 AUC), so weigh effort accordingly.
findings.feasibility: Embedding-plus-shallow-head is fully CPU-feasible; the only heavy step is one forward pass of the encoder per study.

findings.title: HiCur-NPC: hierarchical feature fusion curriculum learning for a multimodal nasopharyngeal carcinoma foundation model
findings.summary: Per PubMed: pretrains visual encoders with a Hybrid Contrastive Masked Autoencoder on 755K multimodal NPC images (CT, MRI, endoscopy), builds a 65K visual instruction-tuning set from open data and clinician reports, and adds a Mixture-of-Experts cross-attention fusion. Reported to outperform prior specialized models on NPC diagnosis, report generation, tumor segmentation and prognosis.
findings.relevance: The closest thing in the literature to an H&N-specific multimodal foundation model, and it covers exactly HNRad's target task mix (segmentation + report + prognosis) in head/neck anatomy. Use as an architectural template and as evidence that H&N-specific pretraining beats generic CT models on H&N tasks.
findings.license: Not stated in the abstract; IEEE paywalled — code/weight availability unknown
findings.feasibility: n/a for direct deployment (no confirmed public weights); MoE cross-attention plus multi-encoder design would be heavy on CPU even if released.

findings.title: Big, Bright, or Invisible: a frozen-feature benchmark of 3D CT foundation models
findings.summary: Benchmarks ten frozen CT encoders on thoracic CT across three cohorts using kNN, zero-shot prompting and linear probing. Finds no universal state of the art — rankings fluctuate with evaluation context — and identifies a physical bottleneck: detectability scales with a finding's contrast against surrounding tissue. Widespread or high-contrast abnormalities are reliably detected; small, low-contrast focal lesions remain a persistent failure across all encoders.
findings.relevance: Direct feasibility warning for HNRad's hardest targets. Small low-contrast findings are exactly perineural spread, subtle cartilage invasion, and early ENE. This says frozen foundation-model features will not solve those, and argues HNRad should keep geometry-based, deterministic tools (encasement degrees, min CSA, Robbins mapping) as the primary product and treat any learned classifier as advisory.
findings.feasibility: n/a — evaluation study. Its linear-probe protocol is itself CPU-cheap and worth copying for local model selection.

findings.title: CT-SpatialVQA: 3D medical VLMs perform at or below chance on spatial reasoning
findings.summary: Benchmark of ~9,100 QA pairs derived from 1,600+ radiology reports (95% human consensus) probing explicit anatomical localization, laterality awareness, structural comparison and 3D inter-structure relational reasoning. Eight 3D medical VLMs average 34% accuracy and are often below random, suggesting reliance on learned priors rather than genuine volumetric understanding.
findings.relevance: The strongest argument against using any current VLM for HNRad's spatial core (roadmap 5 carotid encasement degrees, 7 Robbins level mapping, 9 mandible/canal relations, 10 vascular variants). Laterality errors alone are a surgical safety issue. Compute these geometrically from segmentations and landmarks; do not ask a VLM.
findings.feasibility: n/a — benchmark. Worth reusing its four task categories as an internal sanity test if a VLM is ever added.

findings.title: Sparse concept channels in frozen 3D CT vision encoders (Concept Channel Probe)
findings.summary: Probes frozen embeddings from Pillar-0 and Merlin and finds each radiological finding is encoded by a sparse set of about 10 vision-encoder channels that match full-feature classification performance. The resulting Concept Channel Probe beats published CT-CHAT on clinical efficacy F1 (0.549 vs 0.184) at much lower latency.
findings.relevance: A concrete, CPU-native recipe: extract frozen embeddings once, select ~10 channels per finding, and run a tiny sparse probe instead of a generative VLM. This is both faster and far more accurate than the chat model, and it is inherently auditable — you can show which channels drove a flag, which matters for a surgeon-facing tool.
findings.feasibility: Ideal for HNRad: the probe itself is a handful of floats; all cost is the single encoder forward pass. Also a damning data point about generative CT chat models (CT-CHAT F1 0.184).

findings.title: Anatomy Contextualized Adaptation of CT foundation models (ACA)
findings.summary: Lightweight framework that adapts frozen CT foundation models for anatomy-level vision-language alignment while preserving global context, evaluated on Merlin and CT-RATE. Consistently outperforms frozen baselines in zero-shot finding classification and requires less than one hour of training once embeddings are cached.
findings.relevance: Shows how to specialize a general CT encoder to a specific anatomy (their point is organ-level; HNRad's is the neck) without retraining the backbone. The cache-embeddings-then-train-a-small-head pattern is the only fine-tuning strategy that is realistic on a no-GPU workstation.
findings.feasibility: Sub-hour training on cached embeddings is plausibly CPU-feasible. Encoder forward passes to build the cache are the bottleneck; run them overnight.

findings.title: CheapCT: when do cheap probes predict expensive training for 3D-CT encoders?
findings.summary: Tests whether inexpensive probes of frozen 3D-CT encoders forecast the outcome of full fine-tuning on report generation and a new MeasureVQA dataset. Rank agreement between probe and fine-tuning stays high throughout (Spearman rho 0.90-1.00), enabling encoder selection without paying for fine-tuning.
findings.relevance: Operationally the most useful methods paper for a no-GPU builder: it justifies choosing among CT-FM, Merlin, Pillar-0 and others by cheap linear probes on a local H&N cohort rather than by fine-tuning anything. Directly de-risks roadmap 13.
findings.feasibility: Probing is a matrix solve on cached embeddings — trivially CPU-feasible on 32 GB RAM.

findings.title: ORCA: organ-centroid aggregation for training-free 3D CT visual token compression
findings.summary: Training-free compressor for 3D CT visual tokens evaluated on CT-RATE and Merlin. Reports 64x visual context compression, 50x KV-cache reduction and 31x speedup while improving attribute prediction and report generation.
findings.relevance: If HNRad ever runs a 3D-input VLM locally, token count is the dominant CPU cost. A training-free 31x speedup is the difference between minutes and an hour per study. Also composes with organ segmentations HNRad already plans to compute (roadmap 6/13) since it aggregates around organ centroids.
findings.license: Not confirmed — check the GitHub repo before use
findings.feasibility: Training-free and code released, so adoptable without retraining. Still requires a host VLM; useful only once a 3D VLM is in the stack.

findings.title: MedImageInsight: an open-source embedding model for general-domain medical imaging
findings.venue_or_repo: arXiv 2410.06542; Microsoft (Hugging Face model card is gated — returned 401)
findings.summary: General medical image embedding model reporting SOTA or human-expert-level results across classification, image-image search and fine-tuning, explicitly including CT 3D retrieval and chest X-ray classification, with AUC above 0.9 in most domains. Notably achieves report-generation results using less than 10% the parameters of comparable models.
findings.relevance: A small-footprint embedding model is exactly what HNRad needs for a local DICOM library (roadmap 1) — content-based similar-case retrieval across the surgeon's own archive, entirely on-device, with no generative risk.
findings.license: Unknown — the Hugging Face card is access-gated (HTTP 401) and I could not confirm the license text; verify before use
findings.feasibility: Parameter count not confirmed; the paper's low-parameter claim suggests CPU feasibility for embedding extraction. Gated download may be blocked by the KP corporate proxy.

findings.title: BiomedCLIP (PubMedBERT + ViT-B/16, 224px)
findings.summary: ViT-B/16 image encoder with PubMedBERT text encoder, contrastively trained on PMC-15M (15M figure-caption pairs from PubMed Central). MIT licensed. The card explicitly states that any deployed use case, commercial or otherwise, is currently out of scope, and that the model is not designed for clinical deployment; it is English-only and 2D.
findings.relevance: Commonly proposed as a cheap CPU-friendly medical CLIP, and it genuinely is (ViT-B/16 at 224px runs fine on CPU), but it is 2D figure-caption data with no CT volume understanding, and the authors disclaim deployment. Suitable at most for 2D thumbnail tagging or a UI search over screenshots, not for H&N CT interpretation.
findings.license: MIT (but model card declares deployment out of scope)
findings.feasibility: ViT-B/16 at 224px is comfortably CPU-real-time on 32 GB RAM; pip installable via open_clip. The limitation is scientific, not computational.

findings.title: RadFM: towards a generalist foundation model for radiology with web-scale 2D and 3D medical data
findings.summary: Builds MedMD (16M medical scans with text) and the cleaned RadMD (3M radiologic vision-language pairs) covering 5,000+ diseases, and trains a generalist model accepting interleaved 2D and 3D scans. Reports outperforming OpenFlamingo, MedFlamingo, MedVInT and GPT-4V on the RadBench evaluation across modality recognition, disease diagnosis, VQA, report generation and rationale diagnosis.
findings.relevance: Seminal 3D-capable generalist radiology VLM and a useful comparison point, but superseded on CT benchmarks by Merlin/Pillar-0 and sized for GPU clusters. Reference only.
findings.license: Not confirmed from the abstract page; dataset provenance is web-scale scraped literature, which raises its own reuse questions
findings.feasibility: Large multimodal LLM with 3D input — not CPU-feasible on this workstation.

findings.title: MAIRA-2: grounded radiology report generation
findings.summary: Large radiology-specific multimodal model that generates chest X-ray reports with and without spatial grounding, and introduces RadFact as an evaluation framework for grounded reports. Reports state-of-the-art report-generation performance on chest radiograph benchmarks.
findings.relevance: Relevant only as a design pattern for roadmap 14: grounded reporting, where each generated sentence carries a box/region pointer, is the right safety architecture for a surgeon-facing tool. The model itself is CXR-only and irrelevant to H&N CT.
findings.license: Research-use restrictions apply to MAIRA weights (Microsoft research license) — verify before any use
findings.feasibility: CXR 2D only; no CT. Not deployable for HNRad.

findings.title: GREEN: generative radiology report evaluation and error notation
findings.summary: A lightweight open-source metric for evaluating generated radiology reports that correlates better with expert error counts and expert preferences than prior metrics, and produces human-interpretable explanations of clinically significant errors rather than a single opaque score.
findings.relevance: If HNRad ever auto-drafts tumor board text (roadmap 14), BLEU/ROUGE are worthless for judging it. GREEN gives an error-typed, explainable evaluation that a surgeon can audit. Use it as the acceptance gate for any generated text before it reaches a report.
findings.license: Open-source (specific license not confirmed from the feed)
findings.feasibility: GREEN's scorer is itself an LLM, so local scoring needs a quantized model; alternatively use its error taxonomy as a manual review checklist, which costs nothing.

findings.title: ModaLens: report-conditioned medical VLMs largely stop looking at the image
findings.summary: Paired image-swap audit of MedGemma-27B on 3,199 MIMIC-CXR cases. When the radiology report is supplied in context, swapping the image changes the model's answer only 4.26% of the time, versus 20.94% without the report — a 16.7-point paired increase. Replicated across model variants.
findings.relevance: Critical failure mode for any HNRad design that feeds both the prior report and the images to a VLM: the model will parrot the report and effectively ignore the pixels. That is the worst possible behavior for a tool meant to catch what the report missed (retropharyngeal ICA, aberrant subclavian, early cartilage invasion).
findings.feasibility: n/a — audit method. The image-swap test is cheap to replicate locally as a regression test.

findings.title: Does acceleration cause hidden instability in vision language models? (quantization audit)
findings.summary: Evaluates quantization across LLaVA-1.5, LLaVA-Next, Qwen2-VL and Qwen2.5-VL with case studies on the medical VLM LLaVA-Med. Despite minimal aggregate performance drops, quantized models changed their original answers up to 20% of the time, and up to 6.5% of answer changes flipped correct responses to incorrect ones.
findings.relevance: Directly governs the only realistic local VLM path (4-bit GGUF MedGemma via Ollama/llama.cpp on CPU). Aggregate benchmark parity hides per-case instability, so HNRad must not validate a quantized model on averages alone — test the exact quantization that ships, case by case.
findings.feasibility: n/a — evidence about the deployment method HNRad would otherwise default to.

findings.title: Resolution meets reduction: efficient visual context for 3D radiology report generation
findings.summary: Systematically evaluates vision encoders and token-reducing projectors with 1.7B-4B LLMs on CT-RATE and Merlin, reaching clinical macro-F1 of 49.5 (CT-RATE) and 49.0 (Merlin) using anatomy-guided cropping. Code and models stated to be published upon publication.
findings.relevance: Two useful signals for HNRad. First, anatomy-guided cropping (feed the model only the relevant region) beats brute-force resolution — which suits a neck-focused tool that already segments structures. Second, and more soberingly, state-of-the-art clinical macro-F1 for 3D CT report generation is still roughly 50%, so automated CT reporting is not close to clinical reliability.
findings.feasibility: 1.7B LLM plus a cropped-region encoder is the most plausible size class for future CPU use, but weights are not yet public.

findings.title: VoxelFM: robust visual features in CT via self-distillation for frozen-backbone transfer
findings.summary: Self-distillation pretraining that yields frozen-backbone CT features performing well across seven task categories without any language supervision, positioning language-free self-supervision as competitive with vision-language pretraining for clinical transfer.
findings.relevance: Supports the architecture HNRad should prefer: a frozen vision encoder plus small task heads, with no text model in the loop. Removing the language component removes the hallucination surface entirely while keeping transfer performance — the right trade for a surgical planning tool.
findings.license: arXiv preprint (license not confirmed); weight release not confirmed
findings.feasibility: Frozen-backbone inference is the CPU-friendly regime; confirm whether weights are actually downloadable before planning around it.

gaps: Web search budget for this session was exhausted (200/200 WebSearch calls used) before I started, so all findings come from the arXiv API, Hugging Face/GitHub pages, and PubMed via WebFetch/MCP. I could not run broad Google/Bing-style discovery over Papers with Code, grand-challenge.org, or RSNA/AJNR/Radiology/Head & Neck journal sites, so product-level and challenge-level results are under-covered.

No measured CPU inference benchmarks exist in the literature for any of these 3D CT foundation models. Not one model card or paper reports wall-clock CPU latency or peak RAM for a full CT volume. The CPU feasibility judgments above are inferred from parameter counts and architecture class, not measured. This has to be settled empirically on the actual workstation.

Parameter counts and input volume resolution for Merlin are not stated on its arXiv abstract page, GitHub README, or Hugging Face card; only the Nature 2026 paper would have them, which I could not retrieve.

MedImageInsight's Hugging Face model card returned HTTP 401 (gated), so I could not confirm its license or parameter count. Its license is the deciding factor for whether it is usable for local case retrieval.

Pillar-0's code repository could not be located (github.com/reginabarzilaygroup/Pillar-0 returned 404) and its weight availability, architecture and license are unconfirmed despite it being the highest-performing model in the comparison.

No evaluation of any general CT foundation model specifically on head & neck anatomy for the geometric tasks HNRad targets. The two H&N papers found are both outcome prediction (recurrence, distant metastasis); nothing evaluates these encoders on carotid encasement, Robbins level assignment, cartilage invasion, ENE, or airway geometry.

HPV status prediction, perineural spread detection, and 4D CT parathyroid localization returned nothing in the foundation-model/VLM literature I could reach — these may be covered in the radiomics literature that another agent's topic addresses.

I could not verify whether the KP corporate proxy permits Hugging Face gated-model downloads (MedGemma and MedImageInsight both require accepting terms and an auth token), which is a hard prerequisite for two of the more promising options.
Jolia (huggingface.co/raidium/Jolia) was listed as having released weights for a 3D CT VLM, but I did not fetch its model card and cannot confirm size or license.

sweeps.topic: Public head & neck CT/PET/MRI datasets and benchmarks usable for local, PHI-free validation of HNRad

findings.title: HECKTOR 2022 (HEad and neCK TumOR segmentation and outcome prediction challenge)
findings.summary: ~882 FDG-PET/CT cases from 9 centers (Canada, Switzerland, France, USA) with expert GTVp (primary tumor) and GTVn (nodal) contours, plus clinical data and recurrence-free survival endpoints. Two tasks: lesion segmentation and RFS prediction. Access via Grand Challenge registration and a data-download page; license terms are not stated on the landing page.
findings.relevance: Primary validation corpus for roadmap items 12 (PET/CT fusion SUV/MTV) and 13 (AI organ/tumor segmentation). GTVn contours also give a ground truth for nodal volumetrics and, indirectly, for the Robbins neck-level mapper (item 7) if node centroids are mapped to levels manually.
findings.feasibility: NIfTI-style resampled volumes; PET/CT pairs are small enough (a few hundred MB per batch) to hold locally. Reading and metric computation is pure SimpleITK/NumPy on CPU — no GPU needed for validation, only for training.
findings.license: Not stated on the challenge landing page; registration + participation agreement required. Treat as research-use-only until confirmed.

findings.title: HECKTOR 2025 (3-task edition: segmentation, RFS, HPV status)
findings.summary: Over 1,200 patients from at least 11 centers: the ~850 HECKTOR-2022 patients with refreshed clinical data plus ~400 new patients from two French cohorts. Adds radiotherapy dose maps for the RFS task and a dedicated HPV-status prediction task from imaging + clinical variables. Hosting location for the data is not stated on the landing page.
findings.relevance: Directly supplies labelled data for the two stretch goals the project lists outside the core roadmap: HPV prediction and outcome/recurrence modelling, on top of the same PET/CT segmentation targets as item 13.
findings.feasibility: Same PET/CT handling as HECKTOR 2022. HPV/RFS tasks are tabular+radiomic and run comfortably on CPU with scikit-learn/lifelines; full 3D deep models would not.
findings.license: Not stated on the landing page; challenge registration required.

findings.title: Overview of the HECKTOR Challenge at MICCAI 2022: Automatic Head and Neck Tumor Segmentation and Outcome Prediction in PET/CT
findings.venue_or_repo: Head Neck Tumor Chall (MICCAI 2022 proceedings) — PMID 37195050
findings.summary: Official challenge overview reporting dataset construction, annotation protocol, evaluation metrics and the performance envelope of all participating methods for GTVp/GTVn segmentation and RFS prediction. This is the citation of record for what Dice/HD95 numbers count as state of the art on H&N PET/CT.
findings.relevance: Gives defensible benchmark numbers to compare any local segmentation module (item 13) against, and documents the annotation convention HNRad should mirror when displaying GTVp vs GTVn.
findings.feasibility: n/a
findings.license: Springer LNCS proceedings; abstract open on PubMed.

findings.title: HaN-Seg: head and neck organ-at-risk CT and MR-T1 dataset
findings.summary: 42 patients who underwent both CT and T1-weighted MR for RT planning, with expert binary masks for 30 organs at risk. Single 4.9 GB zip, direct download, no application process. Accompanying HaN-Seg 2023 Grand Challenge reports inter-observer and inter-modality variability.
findings.relevance: The cleanest small dataset for validating OAR segmentation (item 13) and for testing the CT-MR registration path in compare mode (item 11) — same patient, two modalities, shared reference contours. Also gives mandible and carotid-adjacent structures for items 5 and 9.
findings.feasibility: 4.9 GB fits easily in 32 GB RAM workflows; no login, so a corporate-proxy single-file download works. Ideal size for a no-GPU box.
findings.license: CC BY-NC-ND 4.0 — non-commercial AND no-derivatives. Safe for internal validation of a personal tool; the no-derivatives clause means do not redistribute modified masks or derived datasets.

findings.title: SegRap 2023: 45 organs at risk + 2 GTVs on paired non-contrast and contrast CT
findings.venue_or_repo: MICCAI 2023 Grand Challenge; summary paper in Medical Image Analysis 2025
findings.summary: 200 nasopharyngeal carcinoma patients (120 train / 20 val / 60 test), each with BOTH a non-contrast and a contrast-enhanced CT, and 55 pixel-level labelled structures: 45 OARs (optic nerves, brainstem, cochleae, etc.) plus GTVnx (primary) and GTVnd (nodal). Requires a signed end-user agreement; credentials then emailed. Redistribution of data or links is explicitly forbidden.
findings.relevance: The only large public H&N set with paired contrast/non-contrast CT of the same patient — exactly the setup for item 11 (compare mode with registration) and for validating that vessel-dependent features (item 5 carotid encasement, item 10 vascular flags) behave on both contrast phases. 45 OARs is the richest OAR label set available for item 13.
findings.feasibility: Google Drive / Baidu mirrors — the Google Drive route may be blocked by a corporate proxy; plan a manual download. Volumes are ordinary CT, CPU-friendly for metric evaluation.
findings.license: Signed end-user agreement; no redistribution or link-sharing. Effectively research-use-only.

findings.title: QIN-HEADNECK (TCIA) — PET/CT with DICOM SEG, SR and Real World Value Mapping objects
findings.summary: 279 subjects, serial FDG-PET/CT before and after therapy, 201 GB. Uniquely ships standards-compliant DICOM SEG (segmentations), DICOM SR (measurement reports) and RWV (Real World Value Mapping) objects alongside the CT/PT series, so SUV computation and measurement round-tripping can be validated against reference objects. CC BY 3.0, though some face-reconstructible series still route through the NIH controlled-access policy.
findings.relevance: Highest-value dataset for item 12 (PET/CT fusion, SUV/MTV): the RWV objects let HNRad's SUV conversion be checked against a reference rather than re-derived from scratch, and the DICOM SEG/SR objects are ground truth for item 14 (reporting export) and item 6 (segmentation interchange).
findings.feasibility: Native DICOM — parses directly with pydicom, no conversion step. Download a subject subset via a TCIA manifest rather than all 201 GB. DICOM SEG reading needs highdicom or pydicom-seg (pure Python, pip-installable).
findings.license: CC BY 3.0 for the collection; NIH Controlled Data Access Policy applies to face-reconstructible images.

findings.title: PDDCA — Public Domain Database for Computational Anatomy (MICCAI 2015 H&N auto-segmentation challenge)
findings.venue_or_repo: imagenglab (Sharp lab, Harvard/MGH); Raudaschl et al., Med Phys 2017
findings.summary: 48 head and neck CT scans from the RTOG 0522 trial with manual segmentations of mandible, left/right parotid, left/right submandibular gland, brainstem, optic chiasm, optic nerves, plus manually identified bony landmarks. Distributed as three zip files, described as public domain, no application process.
findings.relevance: Smallest, least encumbered dataset with a mandible ground truth — the natural first validation set for item 9 (mandible planner: mandible surface, osteotomy planes) and for item 6 STL export. The bony landmarks also help calibrate the Robbins level mapper (item 7), which is landmark-driven.
findings.feasibility: Tiny by modern standards; trivially handled on CPU with 32 GB RAM. Direct zip download over HTTPS survives most corporate proxies.
findings.license: Stated as public domain / freely provided; citation of Raudaschl et al. Med Phys 2017 requested. Least restrictive H&N option found.

findings.title: TotalSegmentator dataset v2.0.1 (1228 CT, 117 structures)
findings.summary: 1,228 real-world clinical CT scans across many scanners and institutions with voxel labels for 117 anatomical structures, distributed as a single 23.6 GB zip under CC BY 4.0 — the most permissive license of any dataset in this list. The record does not enumerate which head/neck structures are covered; the GitHub repo and paper list the per-structure breakdown.
findings.relevance: Underpins item 13 (AI organ segmentation on CPU): it is the training set behind the TotalSegmentator models HNRad would likely run locally, so it is also the right set for validating that the CPU inference path reproduces published Dice. Contains the great-vessel and skeletal labels relevant to items 5 and 10; H&N coverage needs confirming per-structure.
findings.feasibility: CC BY 4.0 and a plain Zenodo zip — no agreement, no login. 23.6 GB download is the main cost; validation itself is CPU-only. TotalSegmentator inference on CPU is slow but viable (minutes per volume) on Intel UHD-class hardware with the -fast flag.
findings.license: CC BY 4.0 (dataset). Note the TotalSegmentator *models* carry separate, more restrictive terms for some subtasks — check those independently.

findings.title: RADCURE (TCIA) — 3,346 H&N RT patients with GTVp/GTVn and 19 TG-263 OARs
findings.summary: 3,346 head and neck cancer patients treated at University Health Network (Toronto) 2005-2017, planning CT with RTSTRUCT containing primary GTV, nodal GTV and 19 organs at risk standardized to TG-263, plus demographics, TNM (7th ed.), treatment and 5-year follow-up outcomes. 391 GB total, with a 58.55 GB oropharynx-only subset.
findings.relevance: By far the largest labelled H&N CT corpus: the right set for statistically meaningful validation of items 5, 6, 7 and 13, and the outcome data supports ENE/HPV-adjacent modelling. The OPC subset is the practical entry point given local disk limits.
findings.feasibility: CONTROLLED ACCESS — NIH policy applies because the CTs can reconstruct faces; expect an application and approval delay, and confirm KP institutional posture before requesting. Download needs the TCIA Data Retriever (a Java/desktop app) — verify it installs without admin rights, or use the IDC route instead. 391 GB will not fit locally; take the OPC subset.
findings.license: CC BY 4.0 for clinical data; imaging under NIH Controlled Data Access Policy.

findings.title: TCIA HNSCC (MD Anderson) — 627 subjects, CT/PET/MR with TG-263 GTVp and GTVn
findings.summary: 627 HNSCC patients, 309.81 GB, 537,939 images across CT, PET and MR. Includes a Head-Neck-CT-Atlas subset (215 subjects, 99.79 GB) and an Oropharyngeal-Radiomics-Outcomes subset (412 subjects, 55.11 GB) with manually segmented primary (GTVp) and nodal (GTVn) disease named per AAPM TG-263.
findings.relevance: Multi-modal (CT+PET+MR) same-patient data makes this the best test bed for item 11 (compare mode with registration) and item 12 (PET/CT fusion). The CT-Atlas subset is the reference for OAR naming conventions HNRad should adopt in its reporting export (item 14).
findings.feasibility: CONTROLLED ACCESS for imaging (facial reconstruction risk); clinical tables are CC BY 3.0/4.0 and free. Native DICOM, pydicom-friendly. Pull a subset, not 310 GB.
findings.license: Clinical data CC BY 3.0 / CC BY 4.0; imaging under NIH Controlled Data Access Policy.

findings.title: Head-Neck-PET-CT (TCIA) — 298 patients, 4 Québec centers, GTV primary + GTV nodes
findings.summary: 298 patients with pre-treatment FDG-PET/CT plus RT planning CT, 72.46 GB DICOM. RT contours label 'GTV primary' and 'GTV lymph nodes'; 93 patients (31%) were contoured directly on the PET/CT, the other 207 via deformable propagation from a planning CT. Clinical tables include histology, grade, treatment and recurrence/metastasis/survival follow-up.
findings.relevance: This is the source cohort behind much of HECKTOR, but in native DICOM rather than pre-processed NIfTI — which is what HNRad's pydicom-based library (item 1) actually ingests. The 93 directly-contoured cases are the higher-quality subset for segmentation validation (item 13).
findings.feasibility: Native DICOM, 72 GB (subsettable). Controlled access for imaging. The propagated-contour majority means Dice against these masks understates true performance — weight the 93 direct cases.
findings.license: Clinical data CC BY 3.0; imaging under NIH Controlled Data Access Policy.

findings.title: HNTS-MRG 2024 training set — 150 patients, pre-RT and mid-RT T2w MRI with GTVp/GTVn
findings.summary: 150 patients, each with a pre-RT T2-weighted MRI (1-3 weeks before RT) and a mid-RT T2w MRI (2-4 weeks into RT), both with masks labelled background=0, GTVp=1, GTVn=2. NIfTI (.nii.gz), converted from DICOM with DICOMRTTool, ~15 GB, direct Zenodo download with no application. Mix of fat-suppressed and non-fat-suppressed sequences, consistent within a patient.
findings.relevance: The best public longitudinal same-patient dataset for item 11 (compare mode with registration): two timepoints, same modality, same labelling scheme, with real anatomical change between them. Also the only sizeable public MRI ground truth for H&N tumor and nodal volumes.
findings.feasibility: 15 GB, no gatekeeping, NIfTI reads straight into SimpleITK. Registration validation is CPU-only. Note that MRI is outside HNRad's current CT-centric viewer assumptions.
findings.license: CC BY-NC 4.0 — non-commercial. Fine for a personally built internal tool; would block a commercial product.

findings.title: NCI Imaging Data Commons (IDC) — free, login-free DICOM access to 90+ TCIA-derived collections
findings.summary: Cloud-hosted mirror and index of cancer imaging collections, downloadable free and without login via s5cmd manifests or the pip-installable idc-index Python package. Storage and egress are NIH-sponsored. Licensing is per-collection and shown in the portal: ~62.6k records CC BY 4.0, ~26.6k CC BY 3.0, ~6.6k CC BY-NC 4.0, ~540 CC BY-NC 3.0.
findings.relevance: This is the practical ACCESS MECHANISM for item 1 (local DICOM library) on a locked-down workstation: `pip install idc-index` needs no admin rights, unlike the TCIA Data Retriever desktop app, and no-login download avoids the CyberArk/proxy credential problem. Use it to pull CT, PET, RTSTRUCT and DICOM SEG test series.
findings.feasibility: Strong fit: pure-Python pip install, user-level, CPU-only. Two caveats to verify locally — idc-index's Python version support against 3.13 (a 3.11 venv is the fallback), and whether the corporate proxy permits the AWS/GCP S3 endpoints s5cmd targets. Face-reconstructible collections are still gated regardless of IDC.
findings.license: Per collection; filter the portal to CC BY 4.0 / CC BY 3.0 to get unencumbered series.

findings.title: HNC-IMRT-70-33 (TCIA) — 211 uniform-prescription H&N RT plans with 26 normal-tissue structures
findings.summary: 211 head and neck patients who all received exactly 70 Gy in 33 fractions, with simulation CT plus RTSTRUCT, RTDOSE and RTPLAN. 26 uniquely named normal tissue structures with standardized naming, and a supplementary standardized-OAR-name mapping file released under CC BY 4.0. 23.27 GB.
findings.relevance: The CC BY 4.0 standardized OAR naming file is directly reusable in HNRad's structure-name normalization for item 14 (reporting / tumor board export) and item 6, independent of whether the images are ever downloaded. The 26-structure RTSTRUCTs are a compact OAR validation set.
findings.feasibility: 23 GB; imaging is controlled access but the OAR-name mapping table is freely downloadable and is arguably the more useful half for this project.
findings.license: NIH Controlled Data Access Policy for imaging; standardized OAR names file CC BY 4.0.

findings.title: ToothFairy3 (MICCAI 2025) — CBCT with 77 labelled classes including inferior alveolar canal and mandible
findings.venue_or_repo: Grand Challenge / AImageLab-zip; dataset at https://ditto.ing.unimore.it/toothfairy3
findings.summary: CBCT series at 0.3 mm isotropic in Hounsfield units, NIfTI format. The series grew from ToothFairy (2023, inferior alveolar canal only) to ToothFairy2 (2024, 42 classes: mandible, teeth, maxilla, pharynx) to ToothFairy3 (2025, 77 classes adding pulp cavities, incisive nerves, lingual foramen). Training set is public after a sign-up on the DITTO site. Baseline code on GitHub (AImageLab-zip/ToothFairy).
findings.relevance: The only public ground truth for the inferior alveolar canal and per-tooth mandible anatomy — i.e. exactly item 9 (mandible planner: canal tracking, osteotomy placement). ToothFairy2's pharynx class is also usable ground truth for item 8 (airway analyzer) at the oropharyngeal level.
findings.feasibility: NIfTI at 0.3 mm isotropic makes volumes large; expect heavy RAM per case, though 32 GB should hold one at a time. Modality mismatch matters: CBCT HU behave differently from diagnostic neck CT, so a canal detector validated here needs re-checking on MDCT.
findings.license: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 for the training set (non-commercial, share-alike). Sign-up required to download.

findings.title: AeroPath — 27 CT scans with manual airway and lung annotations, MIT/CC BY
findings.summary: 27 CT scans with manual airway and lung labels, deliberately selected for challenging pathology (including obstructing lesions). One folder per patient with CT, airway label and lung label as .nii.gz. Distributed via Zenodo (5.0 GB) and Hugging Face Hub, with a pip-installable demo and a Hugging Face Space. Zenodo record states CC-BY-4.0; the GitHub repo states MIT for both code and data — reconcile before relying on the more permissive claim.
findings.relevance: Closest public ground truth for item 8 (airway analyzer: centreline, minimum cross-sectional area, stenosis). The pathology-heavy selection matches the clinical case that matters — a narrowed airway — better than healthy-volunteer data. Caveat: coverage is tracheobronchial and largely below the larynx, so supraglottic/glottic stenosis is not directly validated.
findings.feasibility: Excellent fit: 5 GB, permissive license, NIfTI, and the whole airway-extraction/centreline pipeline is CPU-viable with scikit-image and SimpleITK. Data also loadable through the `datasets` package.
findings.license: CC BY 4.0 per the Zenodo record; MIT per the GitHub README (code definitely MIT). Verify which applies to the data.

findings.title: Head-Neck-Radiomics-HN1 (TCIA) — 137 HNSCC patients with GTV in DICOM SEG and RTSTRUCT
findings.summary: 137 HNSCC patients, CT (with some PET), GTV delineated by an experienced radiation oncologist and provided in BOTH DICOM SEG and DICOM RTSTRUCT form, plus demographics, follow-up and chemotherapy schedules. Only 11.79 GB. This is the H&N cohort from the foundational Aerts et al. radiomics work.
findings.relevance: Small enough to be the routine regression-test fixture for item 1 (DICOM library) and item 6 (segmentation import/export): having the same GTV as both DICOM SEG and RTSTRUCT lets HNRad verify that its two parsers agree with each other.
findings.feasibility: 11.79 GB is the most manageable native-DICOM H&N set here. Clinical data downloads freely; imaging is controlled access.
findings.license: Clinical data CC BY-NC 3.0; imaging under NIH Controlled Data Access Policy.

findings.title: CPTAC-HNSCC (TCIA) — 207 subjects, CT + MR + PET with linked proteogenomics
findings.summary: 207 subjects with CT, MR and PET radiology (246 GB) plus whole-slide histopathology (97 GB), linked to CPTAC proteomic, genomic and clinical data. Current version 19 (Feb 2025) lists 156 subjects, 466 studies, 3,127 series. Radiology is controlled access; tissue slides are CC BY 4.0.
findings.relevance: Useful only as a secondary multi-modal cohort for item 11 and for any imaging-genomics work touching HPV status; it carries no tumor or OAR contours, so it cannot validate segmentation directly.
findings.feasibility: Controlled access and no contours make this low priority relative to RADCURE or HNSCC. Native DICOM if obtained.
findings.license: Radiology under NIH Controlled Data Access Policy; slides CC BY 4.0.

findings.title: TopCoW — Circle of Willis vessel-component segmentation on paired CTA and MRA
findings.venue_or_repo: MICCAI 2023 Grand Challenge; arXiv 2312.17670; code at github.com/CoWBenchmark
findings.summary: 110 cases (20 MRA from the CROWN subset plus 90 paired CTA/MRA across two batches), with per-component anatomical labelling of the Circle of Willis. Two sub-tasks: binary vessel segmentation and multi-class anatomical labelling. Evaluation code and algorithm templates are public on GitHub.
findings.relevance: Indirect: the anatomy is intracranial, above HNRad's carotid-encasement target (items 5 and 10). Its value is methodological — the multi-class vessel-labelling formulation and the published evaluation metrics are the right template for a cervical carotid/vertebral labelling scheme, and the CTA half exercises the same contrast-phase vessel extraction problem.
findings.feasibility: Small dataset; the CoWBenchmark evaluation code is Python and CPU-runnable. Registration required for data.
findings.license: Not explicitly stated on the landing page; citation of arXiv 2312.17670 requested. Grand Challenge registration required.

findings.title: COSMOS 2022 — carotid vessel wall (lumen and outer wall) segmentation on 3D black-blood VISTA MRI
findings.summary: Sub-millimetre isotropic 3D carotid black-blood MRI (VISTA) with annotations of the lumen boundary and the outer wall boundary, enabling wall thickness, lumen area and percent-stenosis computation. Validation and test sets were distributed via Google Drive and Zenodo to registered participants. Case count is not stated on the landing page.
findings.relevance: Conceptually the closest public resource to item 5 (carotid encasement degrees) and carotid stenosis measurement, but the modality is black-blood MRI rather than contrast neck CT, and the terms restrict use to the challenge itself — so it informs the measurement definition, not the validation.
findings.feasibility: Restrictive terms ('agree not to use the images in any other capacity') make this unusable as a general validation set; case count and current data availability are unconfirmed post-challenge.
findings.license: Challenge-restricted; participants agree not to use images outside the challenge. Treat as effectively closed.

findings.title: OsiriX DICOM Image Library — MANIX head CTA and other named sample studies
findings.summary: Named sample DICOM studies including MANIX (head CTA with contrast, 40 MB), INCISIX (64-slice dental CT, 61 MB), IDEFIX (cerebral angiogram), FELIX (MR aneurysm) and GRUSELAMBIX (coronary angiogram). All are JPEG2000 transfer syntax. Terms are research and teaching only, no redistribution, no commercial use. Downloads now require a valid Premium Membership through a login portal.
findings.relevance: MANIX and INCISIX are the kind of small contrast-enhanced head/neck and dental CT studies useful as viewer smoke-tests for items 1-3 (DICOM library, MPR, volume rendering). Two practical warnings: the paywall now gates download, and JPEG2000 transfer syntax requires pylibjpeg or gdcm on top of pydicom — a good compatibility test in itself, but a likely source of 'file won't open' bugs.
findings.feasibility: Small files, but the Premium Membership requirement plus a login portal behind a corporate proxy makes acquisition uncertain. Prefer IDC-sourced CTAs for routine test data.
findings.license: Research and teaching only; no redistribution, no commercial use. Premium Membership required for download.

gaps: No public dataset with Robbins neck-level (Ia-VI) contours could be confirmed. HECKTOR/RADCURE/HNSCC give GTVn masks but no level labels, so the neck level mapper (item 7) has no direct ground truth and would need a landmark-based validation built from PDDCA bony landmarks plus manual level assignment by the surgeon.

No public dataset with annotated vascular variants (retropharyngeal ICA, aberrant right subclavian, high-riding innominate) was found. Item 10 will likely need prevalence-based validation against published case series rather than a labelled corpus.
No public thyroid or parathyroid 4D CT dataset was located. The SegThy repository URL guessed was a 404 and web search budget was exhausted before an alternative could be found.

No public dataset with per-node extranodal extension (ENE) labels was confirmed. RADCURE and HNSCC carry outcome and staging data that may encode ENE in clinical tables, but this was not verified at the field level.
Perineural spread and cartilage/prevertebral invasion (T-stage descriptor) annotations: no public labelled dataset identified.
Exact license terms for HECKTOR 2022 and HECKTOR 2025 are not published on the challenge landing pages; they must be read in the participation agreement after registration.

Which specific head and neck structures are among the TotalSegmentator dataset's 117 classes was not confirmed from the Zenodo record itself; this needs checking against the GitHub structure list before relying on it for item 13.
AeroPath's data license is stated inconsistently (CC BY 4.0 on Zenodo, MIT on GitHub) and was not resolved.

No upper-airway/laryngotracheal stenosis CT dataset with lumen contours was found; AeroPath covers tracheobronchial airways but largely below the larynx, leaving item 8's supraglottic and glottic range unvalidated.

Whether TCIA controlled-access applications (RADCURE, HNSCC, Head-Neck-PET-CT, HN1) are permissible under Kaiser Permanente institutional policy, and whether the Java-based TCIA Data Retriever installs without admin rights, were not investigated.

The WebSearch budget for this session was exhausted at the first call, so all findings come from direct WebFetch of known dataset URLs plus PubMed. Datasets I did not already know the URL for (e.g. StructSeg 2019, SegRap 2025, newer airway or nodal-level releases) could not be discovered.

It is pure I/O and metadata construction on top of pydicom/NumPy, so CPU-only is a non-issue and runtime is dominated by array copying and file writing (seconds for a 512x512x180 neck-CT SEG; multi-segment fractional SEGs are the slow case, and RLE/JPEG-LS compression of many frames is where to watch for minutes-scale time). It is the correct emission layer for HNRad outputs that must be readable by KP's PACS and third-party viewers — SEG for segmentations, Parametric Map for PET SUV, TID 1500 SR for measurements and tumor-board export, Presentation States for saved layouts — and strictly preferable to hand-rolling those IODs in raw pydicom, where conformance bugs are near-certain. On a UHD 770 with WASM, expect roughly seconds per slice for the vit_b encoder: fine as an interactive per-slice assist, useless as a batch volumetric organ segmenter, so this serves roadmap item (6) but does not replace a TotalSegmentator-class model for item (13). Verify chrome://gpu on the actual KP box and feature-detect navigator.gpu to hide the tool rather than crash. Everything installs as pure npm JS/WASM with no compilers, no CUDA ops and no admin rights, so it is a clear adopt with those two caveats.

CORRECTION 1: vtk-js has NO decimation filter — I enumerated Sources/Filters/{Core,General,Modeling} and found smoothing (vtkWindowedSincPolyDataFilter), vtkCleanPolyData, vtkPolyDataNormals, vtkTriangleFilter, vtkFillHolesFilter, but no vtkDecimatePro/vtkQuadricDecimation equivalent. CORRECTION 2: the API doc claims the writer triangulates non-triangle polygons, but the STLWriter source reads only the first three vertices of each poly (v1,v2,v3) and would silently truncate quads — low-confidence read, and moot because marching-cubes output is already triangles. A 512x512x180 (~47 M voxel) neck CT will block the UI thread for many seconds; I did not benchmark it, so treat that as an estimate, not a measured figure. Mitigations are clean: both vtkImageMarchingCubes and vtkSTLWriter use only typed arrays / ArrayBuffer / DataView with no document/window/fetch dependency, so they run in a Web Worker; crop to the neck ROI and run per-label. Windows/no-admin/no-CUDA is a non-issue (pure pip-free npm wheels-equivalent, WebGL2). Agree with the candidate's advice to target WebGL2 and ignore experimental WebGPU volume rendering.

verdicts.reason: Verified real, permissive, actively maintained, and genuinely admin-free — the strongest feasibility profile of any DICOM-writing option for this project. All candidate claims checked out: repo exists at the stated URL with 284 stars, BSD-3-Clause LICENSE.txt, a confirmed peer-reviewed paper (PMID 29092948), a dcmqi-1.5.7-win64.zip Windows asset, and commits three days old. Two claims needed correction or sharpening. First, the candidate framed this as binaries-only ("sidesteps any Python 3.13 build problems entirely"); in fact there is now a first-class PyPI distribution (added by the Imaging Data Commons wrapper), so the normal install is one pip command into the existing user venv, with the standalone zip as a fallback rather than the primary path. Second, and more important for planning: the candidate's headline relevance claim — that dcmqi gives the Robbins neck-level mapper (item 7) properly coded anatomic regions "rather than free text" — is only half-verified. dcmqi does support AnatomicRegionSequence and segmented-property coded concepts in its JSON descriptor, which is confirmed. What I could NOT confirm is that SNOMED CT / FMA contain distinct coded concepts for each Robbins sublevel (Ia, Ib, IIa, IIb, III, IV, Va, Vb, Vc, VI, VII). dcmqi is the correct plumbing, but sourcing the codes is a separate unsolved sub-problem, and the likely outcome is coded concepts for the broad cervical nodal groups plus a free-text SegmentLabel carrying the exact Robbins sublevel. Budget for that, and do not assume the coded vocabulary exists. CPU feasibility is not really a question: this is a DCMTK+ITK format converter with no inference, no CUDA, no GPU code path. For a 512x512x180 neck CT a multi-segment SEG write is I/O- and packing-bound — seconds, not minutes — with the real cost being file size, since uncompressed binary SEG frames over 180 slices grow with segment count (use dcmqi's compression options). Positioning versus highdicom (the other candidate for item 6): highdicom is pure Python and composes well with pydicom in-process, dcmqi is a subprocess with a JSON contract but has years of conformance testing and reference-standard status behind it. They are not mutually exclusive — dcmqi is the better choice for first light on items 6, 7 and 14 because its output is known-conformant, and it also covers SR TID1500, which is the piece the reporting/tumor-board export will otherwise have to invent. Recommend adopting it as the DICOM SEG/SR writer, with the standalone zip vendored into the project so the pipeline is not hostage to proxy-dependent pip installs.

The core claim holds and is stronger than stated: HNRad needs no Python round-trip for reconstruction geometry, and needs no new dependency at all, because Cornerstone3D already installs vtk.js transitively. I confirmed ImageMarchingCubes, Cutter, ClipClosedSurface, TransformPolyDataFilter, WindowedSincPolyDataFilter and STLWriter all exist at tag v36.4.1 specifically, not only on master. ClipClosedSurface is the standout for roadmap item 9: it caps the clip so an osteotomy cut leaves a watertight, printable solid. Runs entirely in-browser on WebGL2/WASM, which sidesteps the absent CUDA completely and keeps data on-device. Pure JS with no gypfile and no native postinstall, so npm install is user-level with no compilers — the only friction is the corporate proxy. Four corrections to the candidate as written. (1) The URL/package is subtly wrong in a way that will bite: Cornerstone3D depends on `@kitware/vtk.js@36.4.1` (an exact pin), not the `vtk.js` package this candidate names. Installing `vtk.js` alongside it yields two copies of the library with separate class registries, and vtk-js filters validate by class name — STLWriter throws "Invalid or missing input" — so a vtkPolyData built by one copy fails in the other. Import from `@kitware/vtk.js/...` only. (2) Version skew: latest is 37.0.4 but the app is on 36.4.1, so read docs for the pinned tag. (3) The feasibility note's advice to "decimate meshes before export" is not possible in vtk-js — there is no Decimate, DecimatePro or QuadricDecimation in Filters/Core or Filters/General. CleanPolyData only merges duplicate points and WindowedSincPolyDataFilter only smooths; neither reduces triangle count. Real decimation needs an extra library (meshoptimizer WASM or three.js SimplifyModifier) or an itk-wasm pipeline — budget for that. (4) Runtime: ImageMarchingCubes is single-threaded JS, so a full 512x512x180 neck CT (~47M voxels) will take on the order of tens of seconds to minutes and emit a very large triangle count. Crop to a ROI with ImageCropFilter first (mandible or airway bounding box); that is the workable pattern, and on integrated UHD 770 volume rendering of a full CT will be sluggish though usable. Finally, the candidate's evidence_quality of "validated" should be read as engineering maturity, not clinical validation — vtk-js is a rendering and geometry library, not a cleared planning device, so any measurement or osteotomy output still needs the surgeon's own verification.

verdicts.outputs:
Two separately reusable pieces.

(1) Extract Centerline (ExtractCenterline/ExtractCenterline.py) takes a segmentation or surface model and outputs: a centerline curve/model polydata with per-point radius, a branch-split network, and a quantification table (length, curvature, torsion, per-branch geometry). Confirmed algorithm classes, all imported from `vtkvmtkComputationalGeometryPython` / `vtkvmtkMiscPython` / `vtkvmtkDifferentialGeometryPython`: `vtkvmtkPolyDataCenterlines` (Voronoi-diagram centerline), `vtkvmtkPolyDataNetworkExtraction` (fast network mode), `vtkvmtkCapPolyData` (hole capping), `vtkvmtkCenterlineBranchExtractor`, `vtkvmtkMergeCenterlines`, `vtkvmtkCenterlineGeometry`, `vtkvmtkCenterlineBranchGeometry`, `vtkvmtkNeighborhoods` (non-manifold edge detection). README states centerline computation is "typically 5-20 seconds" on simplified input.

(2) Cross-Section Analysis (CrossSectionAnalysis/CrossSectionAnalysis.py) reslices image/segmentation/model along a centerline curve and emits a table + plot with exactly these arrays: MIS_DIAMETER (maximum inscribed sphere diameter), CE_DIAMETER (cross-section equivalent diameter from lumen area), LUMEN_CROSS_SECTION_AREA, WALL_DIAMETER, WALL_CROSS_SECTION_AREA, DIAMETER_STENOSIS (%), SURFACE_AREA_STENOSIS (%), distance along centerline from a chosen origin, and RAS/LPS coordinates. This module imports only vtk/slicer/ctk/qt/numpy — it does NOT call vtkvmtk — so its math is directly portable into the FastAPI backend with plain VTK.

Also present: Vesselness Filtering, Level Set Segmentation, Guided/Quick Artery Segmentation, Branch Clipper, and three Stenosis Measurement workflows (1D straightened-curve distances, 2D segment surface areas, 3D lumen/wall volumes).
verdicts.reason:
Confirmed real, active, permissively licensed, CPU-only, and now genuinely pip-installable on the target machine — and the output arrays are a near-exact match for roadmap item (8).

The candidate's one stated risk is resolved in HNRad's favor. The claim "vmtk itself is often conda-installed — check pip availability on 3.13 or use a 3.11 venv" is now obsolete: vmtk 1.5.0 (July 2026) added cibuildwheel PyPI packaging, and 1.5.1 (released today) ships `vmtk-1.5.1-cp313-cp313-win_amd64.whl`. setup.py builds with `-DVTK_VMTK_WRAP_PYTHON:BOOL=ON`, so the wheel contains the Python-wrapped `vtkvmtk*Python` modules that ExtractCenterline actually calls. `pip install vmtk>=1.5.1` on Python 3.13, user-level, no admin, no compiler, no conda, no CUDA anywhere in the stack.

Architecture fit: do NOT try to embed 3D Slicer. The right pattern is (a) lift the Cross-Section Analysis math into the FastAPI backend — it is pure VTK + numpy, no vtkvmtk dependency, so it is the cheapest high-value port in the whole roadmap; and (b) call `vtkvmtkPolyDataCenterlines` from the pip vmtk wheel in a sidecar venv for the centerline itself. Optionally install portable 3D Slicer + SlicerVMTK at user level as a visual ground-truth harness to validate the port against, which is the cheap way to get validated-against-reference behavior.

Runtime expectation for a 512x512x180 neck CT: the centerline algorithm operates on a surface mesh, not the voxel volume, so the volume size is not the cost driver. Pipeline is threshold/segment airway (scikit-image, seconds) → marching cubes → decimate → centerline. The Voronoi-diagram step is memory- and time-hungry on dense meshes, so aggressive decimation before `vtkvmtkPolyDataCenterlines` is mandatory; with that, expect seconds to roughly a minute on CPU, consistent with the README's 5-20 s figure. 32 GB RAM is comfortable provided you decimate.

Caveats to carry forward, none disqualifying: (1) the PyPI packaging is brand new — 1.5.1 landed the same day as this review and explicitly fixes a 1.5.0 bug that installed vmtk outside site-packages, so pin >=1.5.1 and smoke-test the import before building on it; (2) `vtk==9.6.2` is an exact pin, so isolate it in its own venv; (3) avoid the vmtkmeshgenerator/TetGen path for license reasons; (4) it segments nothing on its own — it needs a lumen/airway mask as input, so it composes with, rather than replaces, roadmap items (6) and (13).

It is the single closest reference implementation for roadmap item 9 and the segmentation-to-STL half of item 6, and it is the right recommendation as an escape hatch for actual guide fabrication while HNRad owns the diagnostic/measurement half. Three corrections to the candidate record, all of which sharpen rather than sink it. (1) The candidate's "Slicer is a portable ZIP install (no admin)" is NOT verified: the Slicer docs I read (getting_started, get_help, about) say only "Run the installer" and never mention portable ZIP, per-user install, or admin privileges. (2) The reusable code is NOT copy-pasteable. (3) The candidate did not mention that BRP now ships AI-segmentation helpers; DentalSegmentatorHelper.py selects `device='cuda' if torch.cuda.is_available() else 'cpu'`, so it degrades to CPU rather than hard-failing on the UHD 770, but nnUNet CPU inference on a sub-millimetre head CT is plausibly tens of minutes and I did not benchmark it, so treat that path as optional and keep manual threshold/scissors segmentation as the default. CPU feasibility for the core tool is not in doubt: all planning geometry is CPU VTK and runs in seconds on a 512x512x180 neck CT; Slicer's stated floor is OpenGL 3.2 and 4-8 GB RAM, which the UHD 770 (OpenGL 4.6) and 32 GB clear easily, with the documented caveat that a discrete GPU is merely "recommended" for interactive 3D volume rendering, so expect sluggish but usable volume rendering. Recommended scope: adopt as a reference implementation and clinical escape hatch, not as a runtime dependency of HNRad.

Segmentation as labelmap/contour/surface with adapter dirs Segmentation, RTStruct, ParametricMap; docs confirm `generateSegmentation()` → DICOM SEG dataset, `generateRTSSFromRepresentation()` → RTSTRUCT, with predecessorImageId revision handling — full round-trip for roadmap 6 and 14. @cornerstonejs/ai (MIT) bundles onnxruntime-web 1.17.1 + dcmjs, giving an in-browser interactive-segmentation (SAM-style) path relevant to roadmap 13, and @cornerstonejs/labelmap-interpolation plus @cornerstonejs/nifti-volume-loader are first-party packages.
verdicts.reason: CONFIRMED and healthy: repo exists at the stated URL, MIT, pushed the same day I checked, v5.10.6 released yesterday. It delivers, in-tree and verified, almost every viewer-layer roadmap item: MPR (VolumeViewport), 3D VR (VolumeViewport3D), the measurement toolset, labelmap/contour/surface segmentation, and SEG/RTSTRUCT/SR export. No CUDA anywhere — rendering is WebGL2 via vtk.js on the integrated GPU, decoding is WASM, install is pure npm with prebuilt codecs, so it is fully user-level on a locked Windows box. Two corrections to the candidate's stated rationale, both worth acting on before committing: (1) the "one shared offscreen WebGL canvas that blits to on-screen canvases" description is now the LEGACY TiledRenderingEngine. The docs state "The ContextPoolRenderingEngine is now the default in Cornerstone3D," and it renders each viewport into its own offscreen canvas using a pool of WebGL contexts, "Default is 7, can be adjusted based on your needs." So the texture-sharing argument for affordability on integrated graphics does not hold as written; on UHD 770 plan to tune the pool size down (3-4 for a 3-up MPR + 3D layout) and benchmark both engines. Shared Volume Mappers still avoid duplicating volume textures across viewports, which is the more important win. (2) Integrated-Intel risk is documented and unresolved: issue #453, "Fix for WebGL Context Lost on Windows Devices with Integrated Intel GPUs," is still OPEN (2023) with only Chrome-flag workarounds (ignore-gpu-blocklist, ANGLE backend) — user-level flags, but possibly locked by KP browser policy. Also relevant: #1986 "GPU memory use is through the roof" (~10 GB GPU for 900 MB heap, closed), #46 WASM allocation failure on Intel HD 530, and #2685 an open feature request for a WebGPU backend stating large datasets are "unusable with WebGL." Concrete gate before building on it: load a real 512x512x180 neck CT (~94 M voxels, ~180 MB as int16, which VTK.js will upload as a 3D float or 16-bit texture) into a 3-up MPR plus a 3D viewport in the actual KP-managed Chrome/Edge, leave it open 30+ minutes, and watch for context loss. If it survives, adopt without reservation; UHD 770 shares system RAM (32 GB available) so texture capacity is less of a constraint than driver stability. Caveats that are not blockers: 523 open issues is high but normal for a project of this surface area; the CPU-rendering fallback documented in early Cornerstone3D no longer exists in the docs tree (no cpu-rendering.md under concepts/cornerstone-core), so WebGL2 is a hard requirement with no software path; and @icr/polyseg-wasm, the optional polymorphic-segmentation dependency, is third-party and its license needs a separate check since the rest of the stack is cleanly MIT/BSD.

verdicts.outputs: (1) A new DICOM RTSTRUCT file written from a reference DICOM series plus one or more boolean 3D NumPy masks (`RTStructBuilder.create_new(...)` → `add_roi(mask=..., name=..., color=[r,g,b], description=...)` → `save('name')`); mask is indexed one 2D plane per slice. (2) Boolean 3D NumPy masks extracted back out of an existing RTSTRUCT ROI (`create_from(...)`, `get_roi_names()`, `get_roi_mask_by_name()`) — the arXiv abstract also advertises SimpleITK Image output. (3) Merged RTSTRUCTs from the same series. (4) `contour_mode="voxel_edge"` (main branch only) places contours on outer voxel edges rather than voxel centres, and a contour-approximation toggle controls polygon simplification. No segmentation, no SEG object, no DICOM SR — it is purely a contour I/O layer.
verdicts.install_notes: `pip install rt_utils` resolves on local Python 3.13.12 (pure py2.py3-none-any wheel; deps pydicom 3.0.2, numpy 2.4.4, opencv-python 5.0.0.93 binary wheel — no compiler, no admin). Gotchas: PyPI is stuck at 1.2.7 (Jan 2023); the orientation/PixelSpacing fix (issue #92) and `contour_mode='voxel_edge'` exist only on main, so prefer `pip install git+https://github.com/qurit/rt-utils@main`. Pulls the junk `dataclasses` 0.6 backport (harmless; `--no-deps` avoids it). The libGL note is Linux-only. Pin `pydicom<3` / `opencv-python<5` if `save_as` errors.
verdicts.reason: Confirmed real, MIT, actively maintained (commits Aug 2026), and genuinely trivial to install user-level on this box — I ran `pip install --dry-run rt_utils` under Python 3.13.12 and it resolved to a pure-Python wheel plus pydicom/numpy/opencv binary wheels with no compiler, no CUDA and no admin. Runtime is negligible: contouring is per-slice cv2.findContours over a boolean mask, so a 512x512x180 neck CT is sub-second and trivially CPU-only; nothing leaves the device. It fills a real gap for HNRad items (6) segmentation/volumetrics, (7) Robbins neck-level mapper and (14) tumour-board export, since radiation-oncology colleagues and treatment-planning systems consume RTSTRUCT rather than DICOM SEG, and it also lets HNRad ingest existing RT contours as priors. Three caveats that shape how to adopt it. First, PyPI is three and a half years stale at 1.2.7 while main is 1.3.1 — install from git, not PyPI, or you inherit known geometry bugs. Second, there are 64 open issues and a visible cluster of alignment/orientation complaints (#92 PixelSpacing, #110 rotation, #114 RTSTRUCT not aligning with CT, #88 row/column order, #87 cv2.fillPoly exception); the rotation-matrix correction landed on main in Jul 2025 but the surrounding accuracy story is not airtight, so any HNRad RTSTRUCT export must be round-tripped against the source volume and eyeballed in the Cornerstone3D viewer before it is trusted for a case. Third, `ds_helper.py` still sets `is_little_endian` / `is_implicit_VR`, which pydicom 3.x deprecates and pydicom 4 will remove — expect warnings now and a small patch later; the package is tiny and pure Python, so patching is low-risk. Adopt as the RTSTRUCT I/O layer, not as a validated geometry oracle.

verdicts.reason: Confirmed real, permissively licensed, and under active development this month (stable 5.12.4 built 2026-09-09; repo pushed 2026-09-15; 2,629 stars). Adopt it exactly as the candidate framed it — as the ground-truth bench and algorithm source, NOT as a shipped dependency or as the product. Three things I verified that matter: (1) No-admin install is well supported but not officially documented. The packaging code in CMake/SlicerCPack.cmake contains "if (NOT Slicer_CPACK_NSIS_INSTALL_REQUIRES_ADMIN_ACCOUNT) ... RequestExecutionLevel user", the installer's registry writes target HKCU (not HKLM), and multiple independent user tracebacks on discourse.slicer.org show the real-world default path as C:\Users\<user>\AppData\Local\NA-MIC\Slicer 5.x.y. A Slicer core developer announced in Jan 2021 that "3D Slicer is now fully portable", and there is a documented workflow of copying the install folder to a USB drive. I could not find the compiled default of that CMake option or an official "no admin needed" statement, hence "likely" rather than "yes"; the residual risk on a CyberArk-locked KP box is application-control blocking the signed .exe, not a UAC prompt. Mitigation: extract the NSIS installer with 7-Zip into a user directory. (2) CPU/integrated-GPU is fine. Documented minimum is OpenGL 3.2 and the docs state "Integrated graphics card is sufficient for basic visualization"; Intel UHD 770 exposes OpenGL 4.6, so MPR, segmentation and Segment Statistics are comfortable, and 32 GB RAM far exceeds the 10x-your-data rule for a 512x512x180 int16 neck CT (~90 MB). The honest caveat: the docs say "Dedicated graphics hardware (discrete GPU) memory is recommended for fast volume rendering", so GPU ray-cast volume rendering on UHD 770 (shared VRAM) will be interactive-but-sluggish at high quality rather than smooth, and CPU-only AI extensions (e.g. TotalSegmentator in Slicer) run in minutes per case, not seconds. I did not benchmark, so treat those runtimes as estimates. (3) The Python boundary is a hard one and should shape how it is used. Slicer runs its own bundled CPython 3.12.10 (SuperBuild/External_python.cmake on main); it never touches the user-level 3.13, and Slicer's Python context is unavailable even from its own PythonSlicer executable for scene-dependent work. So nothing prototyped in Slicer ports by import — it ports by reimplementation against SimpleITK/scikit-image in the FastAPI backend, with Slicer used to generate the expected numbers. That is still high value: use Segment Statistics volumetrics, VMTK centerline/cross-sectional-area output and markups measurements as the regression fixtures for items 4, 5, 6 and 8, so HNRad's own numerics can be validated against a mature, widely cited implementation instead of being trusted blind. Two flags to carry forward: the license's research-only/no-FDA-clearance disclaimer means Slicer-derived numbers are a development reference, not a clinical warrant; and the Extensions Manager requires proxy access to extensions.slicer.org, so plan on manual extension .zip installs if the corporate proxy blocks it.
